Kobo will soon let you upload and sync your own ebooks across devices, for a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:32:16 UTC
02:32:16 KST

Kobo is launching a new monthly subscription service called Stack that lets you upload your own ebooks and documents to the company’s servers where they’ll be synced across multiple devices and apps, including your reading progress, highlights, and annotations. Kobo Stack is similar to Amazon’s Send to Kindle feature that allows users to upload a wide variety of files to their Kindle libraries for free, but Kobo’s version will cost a few dollars each month.
Kobo will soon let you upload and sync your own ebooks across devices, for a price
Kobo Stack is a new monthly subscription service that’s first launching outside the US as part of a big e-reader update.
Kobo Stack is being introduced as part of a major 6.0 update to the company’s e-reader software, which is available in beta now as an optional upgrade ahead of a wider official release. Supported document types include EPUBs and PDFs up to 200MB in size and files can be pushed to Kobo Cloud using a drag and drop interface on the company’s website, or by emailing them to a custom address you get when you subscribe to Stack.
Your uploaded documents are synced and available anywhere you’re logged in to your Kobo account, including the iOS and Android apps, the Kobo website, and the company’s e-readers. Kobo Stack’s e-reader support is currently limited to recent devices including the Clara BW, Clara Colour, Libra Colour, and the Elipsa 2E, but access for older devices “made between 2018 and 2024 will arrive soon,” according to Kobo’s website.
The initial rollout of Kobo Stack is limited to Canada, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, the UK, and Spain, according to details Kobo CEO Michael Tamblyn shared on Threads, but not the US. Canadian pricing is $3.99 per month, while in the UK it’s £2.99 per month. Kobo is offering a free 90-day trial for those wanting to test it out, and there’s a 60-day grace period if you choose to cancel your subscription. That gives you around two months to download and back up any files you’ve uploaded, and to export your notes and annotations. After 60 days, everything will be permanently deleted.
Other features being introduced as part of the new Kobo firmware update include the ability to add multiple library cards so you can borrow books from several libraries through Libby, lower stylus latency on devices with pen support, improved accessibility with even larger font options, and support for EPUB files protected by LCP DRM.

AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:03:13 UTC
02:03:13 KST

When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend.
AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Swipe left if you’re not aligned.
AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Swipe left if you’re not aligned.
“Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’”
Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.”
In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city —, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles —, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene.
Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely.
On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term.
“It’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future”
“A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. Life could change depending on whether the world manages to get AI alignment right, he tells me. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. He tries to have these conversations in person rather than over text, so a date can ask follow-up questions about why he sees the future the way he does.
For now, he’s focusing on finding a partner with whom he enjoys spending time.
When I ask Kyle if he would date someone who works in artificial intelligence or tech, he says that he would have to think hard about it. He believes that a lot of people who work at frontier AI companies are doing things that he considers pretty heinous. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says.
But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance.
“I just don’t think it’s a factor at all. Like, it’s the least [relevant] thing,” says Bryan, who recently started a relationship. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. Despite his day job (and whatever someone like Kyle might think of him for it), he believes that working out more and looking better probably increases someone’s chances of getting a match way more than any AI or non-AI affiliation. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”
Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000. According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO.
AI is reflected in the way the technology is seeping into San Franciscans’ everyday habits — including those that shape relationships, from how people process their feelings to whom they confide in.
Andromeda, who works as an EMT and a registered behavior technician as well as an AI security analyst, says she’s worried about the unintended consequences of talking to AI chatbots, especially for questions about (and possibly the replacement of) human connection. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.”
“Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. She appreciates the role that a chatbot can play to help someone better express themselves. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.”
At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!”
“There are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus”
If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them.
At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person.
“If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” Joseph tells me at The Midway in San Francisco’s Dogpatch district, where hundreds don white bucket hats and dance next to Hugging Face’s round, foam emoji mascot. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.”
He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses, and Bumble will soon phase out swiping in favor of AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking. Joseph says he won’t share the secret sauce of his AI agent on GitHub, but he tells me it’s pretty easy to make one on Claude Code.
“It has been extremely successful. I’m averaging two closed conversions a week,” he says, meaning that he goes on two dates with two different people. The women on the other side don’t know. The point is to meet in real life. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.”
At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals.
Upon reviewing troves of Date-Me Docs for the San Francisco / Berkeley area, I noticed that quite a few people mention “the singularity” as a factor of whether to have kids. The so-called “singularity” is the point of when technology overtakes human control; some have pointed to the development of true artificial general intelligence as the point of no return. According to JJ, many people in AI safety specifically use the Date-Me Docs as a way to meet people.
“Don’t want kids in the pre-singularity future, if there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then,” one document states.
On the other hand, similar to climate doom anxieties, other people are looking at whether having children is ethical amid massive structural changes in society caused by AI.
“Is the world good, getting to a good place, or is it bad? And if it’s good, baby. If not, no baby, because you’re gonna bring a baby into a world full of potential suffering,” JJ says, explaining the train of thought that these Date-Me Doc potential suitors might have. She does not consider herself a doomer, but she is still pressed for her own singularity timeline. (2029, she suspects.) If anything, she jokes that the approaching end times makes her more likely to want a baby around: “If the bomb gets me, I want to be holding a shiny child.”
These existential concerns have translated into a backlash against tech, San Francisco included. “Stop the AI” rallies have spread to events like Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention and OpenAI’s DevDay, with protestors calling out tech companies and their roles in data center development and ICE raids.
“If there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then”
That skepticism has spilled into how people size up a potential match, even at local events designed to bring the Bay Area together. At a pop-up “Date My Friend” pitch event at the Kilowatt Bar in the Mission District on a Saturday evening, a dozen people pitched their friends and exes to a crowd of more than a hundred.
“He works in tech, but he’s unhappy about it,” one person announced to a chorus of cheers. Other people cracked jokes that their PowerPoints were clearly made by humans, not AI.
Annalise Wulf, 26, one of the three cofounders of the “Date My Friend” series, says that although people in San Francisco try to “tech maxx” their lives, more tech workers with crazy schedules are interested in analog, in-person events to go back to the roots of meeting and creating community. “It’s like, ‘I’m here because I’m not using an AI dating app right now. Like I’m trying to do something different,’” Wulf says.
“I do think it’s maybe popular now to be more anti-tech,” says Lucy Segraves, 28, one of the other cofounders. If someone is working for a company that people see as perpetuating war crimes through their technology, she might be more hesitant to date them.
But ultimately, she says, there are more immediate concerns. “As a person with a non-tech job, I never judge someone if they do work in tech,” Lucy says. “Because that’s unfortunately where the money is, and we’re all just trying to make it in life.”

Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory (reuters.com) 12
			
		 	
				Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports:  The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development.
The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November.

Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build U.S. factory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:50:01 UTC
01:50:01 KST

Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.
The 12-year-old, North Andover, Mass.-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.
The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.
Initially, the factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.
6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:34:39 UTC
01:34:39 KST

inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more, has decided to embrace the modding community. In an interview with The Verge, inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell said, “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want.” That “toolbox” includes making the code for devices like the recently teased MPC Sample Key open source, but also offering developers an SDK to make modifications easier and lessen the risk of bricking your beloved sampler.
How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
inMusic is making open-source MPCs, hackable synths, and mod-friendly DJ decks.
While Akai is eager to see what the modding community cooks up, and has started seeding devices to developers ahead of the official release of the Sample Key, the company takes reliability seriously. O’Donnell said the company wants to “make sure that our official software is completely stable and good for an artist on stage.” He can’t have Fred Again going on stage and discovering his MPC is riddled with bugs. But he also wants people to feel comfortable tinkering. “We’ll try to give them a reset button,” he said so “They can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”
The company is planning to make a big splash NAMM, the annual convention of music manufacturers in Anaheim, with Creator Lab, where it will let technically curious musicians get some hands-on time hacking 22 new products from across its brands. That includes products from Moog, that might not seem like a natural pairing for vibe coding because of its analog design. But O’Donnell thinks it can be, “if we open it up correctly.” That will involve building a platform for devs to work around the analog parts of the circuit.
Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, Polyend open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes, and Behringer has also announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller.
The change in the industry has been quick and seismic. O’Donnell said of the need to provide developers tools for hacking inMusic’s products, “I can tell you it wasn’t on our task list five weeks ago. It just all of a sudden has to be on a task list now.”
Of course, not everyone is thrilled. Elektron has expressed mixed feelings about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned linking to hacks and modified firmware from its official forums, though not discussing them generally, citing concerns about the possibility of damaging instruments. A statement posted on its forums says: “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”
While Elektron doesn’t want people posting links to hacked Digitone firmware on its forums, it’s not actively trying to thwart the modding community. The consensus is there’s no going back now that vibe coding has upended the music gear world, and trying to stand in the way would be a mistake. inMusic’s O’Donnell told the Verge, “you can try to wall them off, which is just a losing battle one … and so we want to embrace them.”

The Air and 17e cap at 20W. A 140W charger is wasted on them. Wireless tops out at 25W on most of the lineup: 20W on the Air, 15W on the 17e and 15 Pro Max. Any Qi2 pad gets there with a 30W brick behind it, 35W for the 18. Still the slow lane. An 18 Pro takes about 30 minutes to 50%, double the cable.
† Apple's numbers. ChargerLAB hasn't posted the 18 Pro yet. The Duo's first lab test (iFanr) measured ~45W, 15V the whole way, and 42–45% at 20 minutes, not Apple's 50%. A plain 45W charger matched an AVS one. Apple's 15 minutes needs a 60W charger with AVS (Adjustable Voltage Supply). Apple's $39 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max has it. So does a 70W Mukiya ChargerLAB pushed to 51W. The Anker below lists AVS. Nobody has shown it fast-charging an 18 Pro. Skip AVS and an 18 Pro Max still hits 50% in about 17 minutes. Still not bad.
The Pro starts at $1,199 and charges at 60W. Apple included a 20W charger, one-third speed. I have feelings about this. (The M5 Pro is the first iPad Apple calls fast-charging; the M4 topped out around 35W.) The Air barely takes more than its own 20W brick. A bigger charger buys it nothing. The new mini fast-charges now, 50% in about 30 minutes on 35W or more, and still ships with 20W. Same feelings, smaller iPad.
† Apple's numbers. No lab has posted the new mini yet.
Airs fast-charge at 70W and ship with Apple's 40W Dynamic. The Neo gets 20W for a 30W appetite, the biggest gap in the lineup. The M6 and 15-core M5 Pro get 70W against a 96W threshold, PROLED or not. Since macOS Tahoe 26.4, Apple admits it: an orange "Slow Charger" label in the battery menu. EU and UK MacBooks have shipped with no charger since April 2026. The Ships With column is the US answer.
Ranked by actual impact. Most people worry about #4. They should worry about #1.
"This is the math behind Optimized Battery Charging. Every 10% Apple holds back roughly doubles battery lifespan."
Above 80%, the battery is working its hardest — voltage spikes, chemistry gets stressed, wear accelerates. Apple knows. That's why all five of these exist. Also: USB-C means the device controls wattage, not the charger. A 140W brick on an iPhone delivers only what the iPhone asks for. You can't overfeed it — the device won't draw more than it's designed for. (The USB-PD spec goes to 240W and Framework now ships one; no Apple device asks for more than 140W.)
160W total. Splits shown are for Standard (C1 Priority) mode. AI mode redistributes dynamically. The display shows you exactly who's getting what.
Apple shipped this 5W charger with every iPhone from 2007 to 2019. Then stopped including chargers entirely. Hundreds of millions still in drawers. And yes — it's USB-A, so you need a USB-A to USB-C cable for anything made after 2023. Still in use. Still slow.

Scriptable GeoDNS: Leaving AWS for Bunny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:15:03 UTC
01:15:03 KST

Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
Vincent Bernat
To optimize the performance metrics of this blog, I relied on Amazon CloudFront to serve the assets,1 and Route 53 for the geo-aware DNS2 to direct readers to the closest host serving the content. But Route 53 is expensive: US$0.50 per zone per month, US$0.70 per million geolocation queries, and US$0.75 per healthcheck per month[1], plus US$1 per month for the KMS key[2] needed to sign zones with DNSSEC. When I discovered that Bunny DNS is almost free[3] for up to 500 domains and features scriptable answers, I made the jump! Plus, it’s a European company based in Slovenia.
Bunny CDN#
Bunny.net[4] started as BunnyCDN in 2015[5]. They added IPv6
support in 2017[6]. Switching was uneventful. I don’t bring a custom domain: I
serve the content from the b-cdn.net domain. As I depend on content
negotiation to serve AVIF and WebP images[7], I configure the CDN to cache
each image format separately[8].
I disable logging[9] to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page[10] promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.
The only downside of the bunny.net CDN offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no ETA to share.
Bunny DNS#
Bunny.net introduced their DNS offering in 2022[11] and recently reduced its cost to almost zero[3]. They support geographical routing[12], but a very cool feature is the scriptable DNS[13]: it runs a piece of user-supplied JavaScript on each query to compute the answer.
I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny’s scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the two nearest servers. The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.
const servers = [
  {
    ipv4: "45.90.160.60",
    ipv6: "2a0c:8881:5:100::1",
    latitude: 48.88,
    longitude: 2.22,
  },
  /* […] */
  {
    ipv4: "139.180.162.114",
    ipv6: "2001:19f0:5800:1855:5400:6ff:fef0:4c0a",
    latitude: -33.87,
    longitude: 151.21,
  },
];
const families = { A: "ipv4", AAAA: "ipv6" };
const records = { A: ARecord, AAAA: AaaaRecord };
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const type = String(query.request.queryType).toUpperCase();
  const family = families[type];
  if (!family) return [];
  // Get user location
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  // Build a list of candidates
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s[family], s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest alive servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Return their IP addresses
  return selected.map((s) => new records[type](s.ip, 3600));
}
The above script relies on the
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer()[14] helper, which returns the
closest alive3 server to the user.4 Thanks to Doggo[15], we can
check it works as expected, at least for A:5
$ doggo --gp-from="Amsterdam" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Amsterdam, NL
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  45.90.160.60
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  116.203.18.48
$ doggo --gp-from="Texas" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Houston (TX), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
The most annoying drawback of this method is that a user from Buenos Aires gets both São Paulo (1000 mi, 30 ms RTT) and Ashburn (5200 mi, 140 ms RTT). Most resolvers randomize the order, so the user may pull the web page from Ashburn. We could return only the nearest server—and swap the scripted record with the built-in geographic routing instead. But if the server becomes unavailable, the browser has no alternative until the DNS cache expires. It leaves a short window of unavailability, even with a short TTL.
The HTTPS record solution#
The HTTPS DNS record[19], defined in RFC 9460[20], solves both the availability and the latency issues. Modern browsers query this record to get additional information to reach an HTTP server, including an alternative port and the application layer protocol—HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Each record has a priority. We can ask browsers to contact the nearest server first and fall back to the next one if the first is unavailable:
vincent    HTTPS  1 first.geo  alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  2 second.geo alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  3 .          alpn="h3,h2"
; Bunny DNS must provide the two closest servers as "first.geo"
; and "second.geo" with geographic or latency routing.
first.geo  A      45.90.160.60
first.geo  AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
second.geo A      116.203.18.48
second.geo AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
vincent    A      45.90.160.60
vincent    A      116.203.18.48
vincent    AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
vincent    AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
This looks like the ideal solution! Unfortunately, Chrome ignores any record
whose target is not .[21], hence the last record at priority 3.
Moreover, unlike with a CNAME, Bunny DNS does not return the IP addresses for
first.geo and second.geo in the additional section. The resolver needs to
send a first request to get the HTTPS record, and a second to resolve
first.geo.
HTTPS records are still too new[22] for this use case. Back to the drawing board! 📐
The hybrid solution#
As a compromise, the script returns the two nearest servers if they are at a similar distance from the user. Otherwise, it returns only the nearest one with a lower TTL of 2 minutes.
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s.ipv4, s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Compute the distance to the user for each of them
  const [first, second] = selected.map((s) =>
    GeoDistance.calculate(s, location),
  );
  // If the second one is at twice the distance and at more than 1000 miles
  // from the first, return only the first one with a TTL of 2 minutes.
  if (second > 2 * first && second - first > 1000) {
    return [new ARecord(selected[0].ip, 120)];
  }
  // Otherwise, return both with a TTL of 1 hour.
  return selected.map((s) => new ARecord(s.ip, 3600));
}
We can check it with Doggo. From Chicago, we get only the Ashburn server with a TTL of 2 minutes, while from Mexico, we get both Ashburn and San Jose.
$ doggo --gp-from="Chicago" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Chicago (IL), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     120s   5.161.44.145
$ doggo --gp-from="Mexico" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Queretaro, MX
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
$ doggo --reverse 5.161.44.145 149.28.219.155
NAME                          TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
145.44.161.5.in-addr.arpa.    PTR   7187s  web05.luffy.cx.
155.219.28.149.in-addr.arpa.  PTR   3600s  web07.luffy.cx.
Note
On the live page[23], the map below is interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.
Note
Enable JavaScript to make the map below interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.
This page was brought to you by ???. Check on the map below whether it matches your
location!
The complete code[18] is a bit more complex. It works around
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() supporting only IPv4, and it handles the case
where there are not enough alive servers to build an answer.
Bunny.net has a comprehensive Terraform provider[24]. I leverage CDK Terrain[25] to build the target state in TypeScript and OpenTofu[26] to deploy it. Have a look at “Managing infrastructure with Terraform, CDKTF, and NixOS[27]” for more details.6
ACME DNS with Hickory DNS#
Route 53 covered one additional use case of mine: serving acme.luffy.cx to
solve DNS-01 ACME challenges[29]. Unlike Route 53, Bunny DNS cannot
restrict access to a single zone with a fine-grained access policy. As this
usage requires neither high availability nor low latency, I replaced Route 53
with Hickory[30], a memory-safe DNS server written in Rust. It supports
automatic DNSSEC signatures[31] and dynamic updates[32]. Its
configuration is simple:
[[zones]]
zone = "acme.luffy.cx"
zone_type = "Primary"
[zones.stores]
allow_update = true
type = "sqlite"
journal_path = "acme.luffy.cx.sqlite"
zone_path = "acme.luffy.cx.zone"
# Private key to sign the zone with DNSSEC. Generated with:
#  openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256
[[zones.keys]]
algorithm = "ECDSAP256SHA256"
key_path = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.pem"
# TSIG key to sign zone updates. Generated with:
#  openssl rand 32
[[zones.stores.tsig_keys]]
algorithm = "hmac-sha256"
key_file = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.update.acme.luffy.cx.tsig"
name = "update.acme.luffy.cx."
The provided zone file[33] only seeds the database on first start. I delegate
DNS-01 challenges to this zone with CNAME records:
_acme-challenge          CNAME bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
_acme-challenge.vincent  CNAME vincent.bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
Lego[34], the ACME client I use to get certificates from Let’s Encrypt[35], answers the DNS-01 challenge by pushing entries with the DNS UPDATE protocol[36].
Unfortunately, Bunny DNS cannot publish a DS record in a zone.7 I need one
to secure the acme.luffy.cx zone and certificate delivery. Therefore, I host
the luffy.cx zone on deSEC[37],8 a free DNS hosting service run by a
non-profit organization based in Berlin. I derive the DS record to publish in
luffy.cx from the DNSKEY record of acme.luffy.cx:
$ ZONE=acme.luffy.cx
$ dig @nsupdate.luffy.cx $ZONE DNSKEY +noall +answer \
>   | dnssec-dsfromkey -a SHA-256 -f - $ZONE
acme.luffy.cx. IN DS 55628 13 2 4946E7508F20E15F1B577A231104B029A1A82E04699A80CD46ADCE31227EE81F
Overall, I am quite happy with the switch to bunny.net. There are still a few
rough edges, like the inability to publish DS records, the lack of HTTP/3, and
the IPv4-only RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper. The bill went from US$5
per month to US$1. So far, performance is on par with AWS[39], but I
only finalized the current setup, including the server in Sydney, in late
October. I need a bit more time to gather more data, and I’ll post a short update. 📈

Promethevs: Full DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017, locally, on 12GB of VRAM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:14:47 UTC
01:14:47 KST

The original model, not a smaller copy · 64 GB of RAM and one 12 GB NVIDIA card · free and open source
PROMETHEVS runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, one of the strongest open models, from all 510 GB of its original weights, on an ordinary PC that cannot even load it: a Ryzen 9 3950X with 64 GB of DDR4, an RTX 3060 with 12 GB and two NVMe drives.
The PROMETHEVS engine gets there with compress-then-correct, a method devised by Ryan Flavell. Every word is first computed on a 2-bit copy of the model's experts. When the model itself is unsure (its top two choices are close), that word is recomputed with the original weights, rebuilt exactly from a stored correction plane. You get close to the speed of the compressed copy and close to the answers of the full model.
- Full-model quality, counted. On 960 audited words the output picks the full model's word 98.3% of the time (the 2-bit copy alone: 97.4%).
- Up to 7.4 tokens/s on a code prompt (warm cache, best case), against 2.14 for running the full model exactly on the same PC. Server runs: 5 to 8 on code, 4.5 to 5.4 on reasoning and agent prompts.
- Fast follow-ups. Only the first read of a long prompt is slow; the engine keeps what it has read, so the next message in a conversation starts in about 2 seconds.
- Works with your tools. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on localhost, with streaming and tool calls, so apps and coding agents that speak the OpenAI API can use it.
- Private. The model runs on your PC; your chats stay there.
- Built from the original weights, on your machine. The installer downloads DeepSeek's weights and builds every store itself, checked against published hashes, so you do not have to trust our files.
- Free. Engine Apache-2.0; report, figures and logs CC BY 4.0.
New here? Check what you need, then install.
The hardware check in the bundle tests all of this and tells you up front if anything falls short. The full list is in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md.
- Download PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip from the latest release and extract it, for example to C:\promethevs_pkg.
- In PowerShell, from that folder:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\check_hardware.ps1        # checks the PC, picks the drives
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_stores.ps1 --run    # downloads the weights, builds the stores (resumable)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\start_engine.ps1          # starts the engine (about 1 minute)
python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed                                # checks it and measures the speed
- Point any OpenAI-compatible app at http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1, model deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-promethevs, any non-empty API key. Close other programs that use the graphics card first.
Every step, the time and disk each one takes, and the known gaps are in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md. Release notes: engine-0.2/RELEASE_NOTES_0.2.md.
Measured on the build machine, 160 new tokens per prompt, two passes per run. Cold is a pass that starts with an empty expert cache. Warm is the second pass of the same prompt with the cache kept from the first, which is the best case for a cache; a real session that sends a different prompt lies between the two. Every individual run is in RESULTS.md.
Agreement is measured word by word against the word the exact path would choose given the same history. A slip is a difference the engine did not check, because the model was confident; the unchecked count counts those. Counting every difference also includes the words the engine checked and deliberately kept at a near-tie (both words almost equally likely). On its own the 2-bit copy picks the full-weight word on 97.4 percent of words; with the corrections, 98.33 percent counting every difference (99.17 percent by the unchecked count). The engine differs from the baseline build in two ways: it holds the draft head's experts in the 2-bit format too, and it keeps the expert cache from the first pass into the second. Keeping the cache lifted the code prompt but not the reasoning or agent prompts (the report gives the round timers behind this). In all three warm code passes no correction overturned a word, so the cache, the 2-bit draft head and the absence of an overturn are not separated, and 7.4 is a best case, not a typical session.
The PROMETHEVS engine does four things at once.
A 2-bit copy answers every word. The experts are stored in a 2-bit format that is smaller than the original FP4, so each word needs fewer bytes from disk. That is what makes the machine fast enough to be useful.
The model's own confidence picks the words to redo. For each word the engine looks at the gap between the model's top two candidates. When the gap falls below a threshold, the gate (0.45 here), the word is flagged.
Flagged words are corrected exactly. A stored correction plane turns an expert's 2-bit copy back into the exact FP4 expert, so a correction is the full model's answer for that word.
A draft head proposes several words at a time. DeepSeek ships a draft head with the model. The engine checks its guesses together in parallel lanes, which spreads the cost of reading experts across several words. The experts the model uses most sit in GPU memory; the rest live in RAM and on the two drives.
The method is compress-then-correct, devised by Ryan Flavell; the PROMETHEVS engine is built around it. Speculative decoding, quantised drafts and offloaded mixture-of-experts inference are the work it builds on; the report sets the method beside the closest references.
The build machine is a Windows 11 desktop with 64 GB DDR4, an RTX 3060 12 GB, and two NVMe drives (2 TB and 1 TB). The stores need about 1,009 GiB: 475 GiB of raw weights plus 534 GiB of derived stores (2-bit copies, correction planes, and FP4 copies of the first layers). Disk is the largest barrier for anyone repeating this. We kept each drive below about 90 percent full.
Every number above comes from one PC. If you run release 0.2 on your own machine, please send the output of python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed and your engine log as a benchmark report. Reports are added here as they arrive.
Frontier-level AI today needs either a cloud subscription or hardware costing tens of thousands of pounds. Open-weight models are closing the gap with the closed frontier models, but running them still means someone else's server. PROMETHEVS, named after Prometheus, who in the myth brought fire to people, sets out to change that: frontier capability, at a speed close to the cloud, within 97 percent of what the original full weights would say, on a computer people already own. Release 0.1 published the method and every measurement; release 0.2 lets you run it.
Ryan Flavell. Compress-then-Correct Decoding: The Full DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on a Five-Year-Old Gaming PC. PROMETHEVS Technical Report 1, version 0.1. MAGNVS Ltd, October 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.23577839
The report (PDF, Markdown) sets out the method, the measurements, where the time goes, what did not help and the related work. Every run behind it is listed in RESULTS.md, with the unedited logs in logs/.
- The technical report (PDF and Markdown) and its figures
- The logs behind every number in it, unedited (RESULTS.md lists them)
- The commands we ran to build the stores and the measurements (REPRO.md)
- Since 0.2: the engine server, its proxy, the hardware check, the store builder and the install check, as PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip on the v0.2 release (docs in engine-0.2/)
- A source rebuild that reproduces the shipped engine program byte for byte (0.2 ships it prebuilt, with its frozen build inputs; see gaps G1 and G2 in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).
- A clean install of 0.2 on a second machine has not been run yet.
- Other platforms: 0.2 runs on Windows with one NVIDIA RTX 30 or 40 series card, and serves one request at a time.
- A reproduction on a second machine, and a demo of a real agent session.
We measured agreement against our own exact path; we have not yet run DeepSeek's reference implementation side by side. Speeds vary by prompt and by run, so we give every run. No prompt reaches the 8 tokens/s milestone we set, and the reasoning and agent prompts run below 5.3. First-word time on long prompts is read-bound: on a 1,163-token prompt the first word arrives after about 126 s (98 s with a candidate prompt-reading setting whose effect on quality we have not fully measured). The 99.17 percent figure covers three prompts of 30, 76 and 1,163 tokens. On a further 1,101-token agent prompt the engine scores 97.80 percent and the baseline build 97.16 (9 slips in 317 words), 0.16 points above our 97 percent contract at the gate we use (at gate 0.30 it falls to 96.21 percent); on a 4,288-token prompt the engine scores 100 percent and the baseline build 99.69. Counting every difference, both builds fall below 97 percent on the 1,101-token prompt (95.91 and 95.58 percent). Each long-prompt audit is one run. The chat template matches DeepSeek's encoder on six plain conversations; tool results and thinking mode are unchecked. All numbers come from one machine, one model and one prompt family.
REPRO.md outlines the steps we ran: download and verify the weights, build the stores, set the profile, run the benchmark. The scripts themselves ship in release 0.2 (PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip, see engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).

Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:05:36 UTC
01:05:36 KST

Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.
Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.
“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”
For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.
Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.
The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.
