 your code:   tkinter   Qt   components   Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust)   Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks   JS / React
                  │      │        │                │                                  │                                    │
                  └──── Python: options, signals    │ ImGui core + BUI backend          └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘
                                  │                │                                  │
 C kit (kit/):   node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr
                                         │
 renderer:       damage-driven software raster (parallel)   or   GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in)
                                         │
 window:         native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window   ·   stdlib Tk window   ·   headless (tests, screenshots)
- Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change.
- The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules.
- The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask.
- Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all.
What's under the hood:
- Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's
interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape
tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects,
text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo,
float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the
kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's
own.
- One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation.
- Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen.
- Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs.
More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works.
These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender
widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and
JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's
Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget.
- Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value.
- Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10.
- Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator
(expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and
sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text.
- Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates,
Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy,
Paste and Reset.
- Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke.
- Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder.
- Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer.
- Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first.
- Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step.
- Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need.
- Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay.
Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets.

BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels.
- The software raster (gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c) is the default. It draws
anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget
shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32
tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in
parallel bands on Windows (BUI_RASTER_THREADS). It needs nothing from your
graphics card and uses the least memory.
- The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows
(gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux
(gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing:
each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame
is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases.
Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on
Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL, libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL
for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU
where OpenGL is missing.
The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends.
Turn the GPU on:
BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the
app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets
it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU
(BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why).
Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon).
More: Rendering.
Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window.
- A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow).
- Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window).
- If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer.
- Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles.
- The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing.
- Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each
rectangle with XPutImage, Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty
rectangles).
On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering.
A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input.
BUI_UI_SCALE=1.5 fixes the UI scale instead of following the display (1 is
Blender's default, 20 px widgets). More:
Window hosts.
Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's:
- Inter, Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1.
- Rendered like Blender's BLF: BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders
with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical
size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text
shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF, stb_truetype rasterizes instead.
- On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with
Slug by default, or from a per-glyph
atlas like Blender's (BUI_SLUG=0, bui.set_slug(False), .slug(false), BUI_gpu_set_slug(0)).
- Other fonts: BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a
folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files.
- Windows' GDI text is opt-in (-DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON, Rust feature gdi-text): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug.
Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), no IME, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback and IME are coming soon. More: Text and fonts.
BUI looks like Blender because it uses Blender's theme. It ships two:
Blender's Dark theme (the default) and its Light preset. Both are
generated by tools/gen_theme.py from Blender's own Blender_Dark.xml and
Blender_Light.xml presets, over Blender 5.x's built-in defaults. Switch at
run time, and every open window relayouts and redraws:
Widgets, panels, the region background, the styled HTML sheet and ImGui's
Blender style all follow the theme. Plain HTML keeps a browser's look either
way. Inside each theme you can still color things yourself: bg / fg in
tkinter, setStyleSheet in Qt syntax, color= on components, full CSS on
HTML in Rust and JavaScript, ImGui's own style colors.
BUI also includes Blender's icons: all 781 of Blender's SVG icons, rasterized with Blender's NanoSVG code so
they're sharp at any scale. Use them by Blender's name: Button("Add", icon="ADD"), EnumRow(..., icons=[...]).
Coming soon: loading any Blender theme file, beyond Dark and Light. More: Theming.
pip install blenderui gives you four APIs in one package:
- tkinter syntax (blenderui.tksyntax): every public tkinter and ttk name
(7,846 of 7,846). Run existing programs with blenderui-tk app.py, or call blenderui.tksyntax.install() first. messagebox and simpledialog are
Blender-styled, colorchooser is Blender's color picker, and filedialog is Blender's File Browser (BUI_FILEDIALOG=native for the OS dialogs).
Look-only Tk options (relief, ttk.Style ...) are accepted, but the look
comes from Blender's theme. Guide: docs/tkinter.md.
- Qt syntax (blenderui.qtsyntax): widgets, layouts (box, grid, form,
stacked), signals, QPainter, menus, timers and animations, QFileDialog as Blender's File Browser. Partial: model/view classes, docks, toolbars,
splitters and Qt stylesheets are missing. Guide: docs/qt.md.
- Blender components (blenderui.components): 45 components, from NumberSlider to NodeEditor. Reference:
docs/components.md.
- Dear ImGui (blenderui.imgui), pyimgui-style. Guide:
docs/imgui.md.
You can mix them in one process: windows, timers and the event loop are shared
(bui.host). Every interaction runs in C, so tests can drive widgets headless.
On the website: tkinter,
Qt syntax,
components,
headless testing.
The blenderui crate is a web-like framework drawn by BUI: every HTML element,
CSS, Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!) or gpui-style builders,
components and hooks. A taste:
rsx! {
    // Tailwind as attributes, any variant, arbitrary values; typos fail to compile
    <button px-3 py-1 rounded-md bg-zinc-800 hover:bg-sky-600 md:dark:hover:bg-sky-400
            active:style="transform: scale(0.97)" onClick={move || save()}>
        "Save"
    </button>
    // control flow right in the markup
    <ul>{for item in items { <li class="py-1">{item}</li> }}</ul>
    {if dirty { <p text-amber-400>"Unsaved changes"</p> }}
    // real CSS, evaluated by the engine
    <div style="width: calc(100% - 2 * var(--gap)); background: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 60%, white)" />
}error: rsx!: `bg-sky-50O` is not a Tailwind utility; did you mean `bg-sky-500` or `bg-sky-50` or `bg-sky-100`?
What's in the box:
- Layout by taffy: block flow and
wrapping text, flexbox and grid (every property, including
grid-template-areas and named lines), tables, relative / absolute / fixed positioning (fixed boxes are placed against the window), scrolling,
and bidirectional text.
- CSS: selectors level 4, nesting, @layer / @media / @supports / @scope / @container / @font-face / @property, var() and env(),
every math function, CSS Color 4 and 5.
- Effects and animations: @keyframes animations and transitions (every
longhand, cubic-bezier(), steps(), linear(), interruptible
transitions), filter and backdrop-filter, mix-blend-mode, clip-path,
masks, 2D transforms, border-image. Frames render only while something
moves, and headless windows step a virtual clock (App::advance_clock).
- Tailwind CSS v4, compiled on first use, with compile-time checks in
rsx! and tw!.
- Components and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style, with optional props and keys.
- Blender components, styled, and the theme.
- Headless testing: Application::headless(), screenshots, simulated
input.
Not yet: async resources (use_resource), generic components, 3D
transforms, OpenType features, multi-column layout. Guide:
docs/rust.md, crate README:
bindings/rust/blenderui, and the website's
Rust section (including
effects and animations).
- @blender-ui/react: a React 19.3 renderer. HTML host components, CSS and
Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and the Blender components.
Hooks keep React's names but hold signals: pass one into JSX and a change
updates that node without re-rendering. README:
bindings/react.
- @blender-ui/svelte: Svelte 5 components (runes, snippets, bindings,
keyed blocks, context, scoped <style>) and the Blender components, on
Node.js (--import @blender-ui/svelte/register), Bun and bui build.
README: bindings/svelte.
- @blender-ui/native: a DOM-like API (createElement, appendChild, addEventListener, className with Tailwind, style) with signals, memo, effect and batch. README: bindings/node.
- How it's fast: BUI renders on its own UI thread, so it never blocks JavaScript; each tick sends one batch of changes; styles are parsed once.
- Standalone apps: npx bui build app.jsx makes a ~7 MB executable with
an embedded QuickJS engine; --bun makes a Bun executable instead; npx bui run app.jsx runs on QuickJS without building.
- Tests: new App({ headless: true }) renders off-screen, and win.click(x, y) simulates input.
Limits: npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 only; events reach
JavaScript after BUI handled them (no native preventDefault), and
event.target is the deepest listening element. Guide:
docs/javascript.md; website:
React,
native API,
signals,
standalone executables.
The C, Python and Rust bindings are generated from imgui.h. ImGui is
idle-free on BUI: frames run only on input and while something animates.
The Blender-widgets build (BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON, Rust feature
blender-widgets) swaps in Blender's widgets, and can be switched at run time
(ImGui_ImplBUI_SetBlenderWidgets, imgui.set_blender_widgets). In that
build, window title bars, tooltips, plain popups, tables and the color picker
keep ImGui's drawing.
Guides: docs/imgui.md, bindings/imgui/README.md (the backend and the Blender style), bindings/imgui/blender/README.md (the widget mapping), and the website's Dear ImGui section.
The kit's concepts: nodes made by type name (frame, slider, button,
panel, tree, canvas, filebrowser ...), properties set by name,
Tk's geometry managers (pack, grid, place) in C, a context that owns
input, popups, focus and undo, a host that receives events, and
windows. A custom node draws and handles input itself; Dear ImGui runs
on BUI that way. Guide: docs/c-api.md.
To embed BUI in your own renderer, render the kit into a BuiRaster and blit
it (as bui.qt.BuiCanvas does inside Qt). A separate, lower-level layer,
render sinks (api/bui_c_api.h), hands the triangles, lines and text of
the immediate-mode GPU seam to your renderer; the Qt/QPainter backend and the
SVG recorder use it. Guide: INTEGRATION.md.
These numbers were measured on a Ryzen 7 5800U laptop (Windows 11, on AC power) before the latest features landed: Dear ImGui, the Linux GPU renderer, the light theme, and the Blender search and expression code. They show the shape of things, not a promise for your machine. Rerun them with the tools in Run the benchmarks yourself.
The same small settings window (a label, text field, checkbox, slider and
button) written each of the five ways, from bench/apps, on
BUI's CPU renderer (the default) and its GPU renderer (BUI_GPU=1). The last
rows are one gpui-syntax source file,
settings.rs, compiled unchanged
against blenderui, Zed's gpui and
gpui-fast. gpui has no form widgets,
so there the controls are styled divs.
Median of 10 launches, from process start until the first frame is on screen, with Python 3.14 and Node 22:
On the same code, blenderui shows its first frame about 5× sooner than gpui and gpui-fast, spends about 8× less CPU getting there, and on the CPU renderer uses half the memory. Idle, gpui keeps about 1.2 % of a core busy; blenderui uses none.
Laptops can't report energy per app, so battery cost is measured by the CPU time an app causes: the CPU it spends starting up, and the CPU it uses over 20 seconds while the window sits idle (what drains a battery while an app is open). BUI redraws only when something changes and otherwise sleeps, so idle use is near zero on either renderer. The GPU renderer starts a little slower and uses more memory (the GPU device), and pays off on large, animated scenes (below). Node's event loop accounts for the JavaScript idle figure, Python's times include starting the interpreter, and memory doesn't count GPU memory.
Python and C, on the full component demo (520×900):
Dear ImGui's demo window with every section open (27k triangles, 1280×800) is a full software redraw of about 5–8 ms.
Rust, against Zed's gpui and the faster fork gpui-fast. The scene is 3000 animated cells, and all apps ran in the same session (GPU rows on Direct3D 11):
Full results, the GPU renderer, and the method
The GPU renderer is off by default. Turn it on with
Application::new().gpu(true), tk.Tk(gpu=True), bui.set_gpu(True) or
BUI_GPU=1:
- Every primitive is one instance of a single shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux).
- Text and images are cached in atlases.
- Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw.
- On Windows, presentation uses a flip-model swap chain with dirty rects.
Its shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends.
gpui-fast's heavy-scene frame rate varies between sessions on this laptop (30–60 fps), so compare within one session. Method, raw data and how to rerun: bindings/rust/bench/README.md.
Startup. These launch a small React app (the counter above) that quits once
its first frame is on screen. Each figure is the median of 12 launches after a
warm-up launch (node bench/startup.js).
First frame is measured from the runtime's start. Launch to exit is wall time measured from outside, including process creation and teardown.
Animation. The same scene as the Rust table above, in one mode: one cell
changes per frame, GPU renderer, medians of 3 runs. CPU is the whole process,
counted with the cycle counter as for Rust.
- Plain JS uses @blender-ui/native.
- React with signals passes the changing values as signals, so the grid renders once.
- React with state re-renders the grid every frame.
- React's production build is used throughout.
What this means:
- JavaScript costs little over Rust: 0.4–2.4 ms per frame, for sending changes to BUI's UI thread.
- Signals make React as cheap as the plain API: the component doesn't re-render.
- QuickJS starts fastest and uses the least memory, from a 7 MB file. It
has no JIT, so re-rendering a 3,000-element list every frame drops it to
20 FPS. Keep big lists on signals, or build with --bun.
React and Svelte, side by side (one session, runs interleaved, medians of
3; --svelte in the commands below):
- Every variant ran at 26–29 FPS in this session (the machine, not the code), so CPU per frame is mostly BUI's own rendering and differs within noise. "JavaScript per update" is the cost of one update alone: 500 back to back, each applied by the framework and sent to the UI thread.
- Svelte with signals costs what React with signals does: a BUI signal
passed as a value ({label}, style={style}) binds its node, so an
update skips Svelte. Before this release's work it went through Svelte as a
store: 86–87 µs on Node.js and Bun, 793 µs on QuickJS.
- Svelte with runes pays Svelte's flush, which walks the component's effects (3,000 here): 65–76 µs, 790 µs on QuickJS (85 / 78 / 790 before).
- Memory: Svelte keeps 10–17 MB more than React with signals (6 MB less than before on Node). A heap snapshot puts the rest in Svelte's own effects, closures and each-block items, about 1.9 KB per cell; BUI's nodes are the same for both.
- Startup: register serves Svelte's runtime bundled (once, with Bun,
into node_modules/.cache), which brought Node.js from 393 to 135 ms and
Bun from 203 to 121 ms. React and Svelte ran one after the other here.
- React with state on Bun and QuickJS: the 500 back-to-back re-renders overran the warm-up, so only its per-update cost is valid from this session. Bun also sometimes crashes when a React app quits (after its first frame), a bug that predates this work.
Method, the memory breakdown and how to rerun: docs/javascript.md.
Every number above comes from a tool in this repo. Build in release mode, close other heavy apps, and plug the laptop in. Run one benchmark (and one build) at a time.
Start time and battery: the five ways and gpui (bench/, Windows). The
same settings window written each way, on the CPU and the GPU renderer, plus one
gpui-syntax file compiled for blenderui, gpui and gpui-fast. It reports start
time, CPU used to start, memory and idle CPU, and writes bench/results.json.
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build --config Release --target buipy  # Python extension
cd bindings/node && npm run build && cd ../..                                # Node addon
cd bindings/rust && cargo build --release --example bench_app && cd ../..    # Rust app
cd bindings/rust/bench && cargo build --release --bins && cd ../../..        # gpui comparison
py -3 bench/run.py 10 20        # launches per app, seconds of idle measurement
Frame cost: 100, 1,000 and 3,000 animated cells, against gpui and
gpui-fast (bindings/rust/bench/, Windows). A 1000×800 window filled with N
rounded, numbered cells, in three modes:
- anim: every cell changes every frame, the worst case.
- one: one cell changes per frame, like a hover or a ticking value.
- idle: nothing changes.
Each app measures its own CPU cycles, frames and memory, and run.py adds GPU
utilisation and GPU memory from Windows' performance counters.
cd bindings/rust/bench
set GPUI_FXC_PATH=C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\bin\10.0.19041.0\x64\fxc.exe   # gpui needs fxc.exe
cargo build --release
py run.py --reps 3                                   # all apps, 100 / 1000 / 3000 cells, about 12 minutes
py run.py --cells 3000 --apps blenderui,blenderui-gpu --reps 1
target\release\bui-bench --cells 3000 --mode anim   # one run by hand (--mode one / idle, --uncapped)
set BUI_GPU=1 && target\release\bui-bench --cells 3000 --mode anim   # on the GPU renderer
Method and full results: bindings/rust/bench/README.md.
JavaScript: the same cells, and startup (bindings/node/bench/):
cd bindings/node
node bench/cells.js 3000                       # DOM-like API, one cell changing per frame
node bench/cells.js 3000 --react               # React re-rendering the grid
node bench/cells.js 3000 --react --signals     # React with signals: no re-render
node --import ../svelte/register.js bench/cells.js 3000 --svelte   # Svelte, runes
node bench/cells.js 3000 --gpu                 # on the GPU renderer
bun bench/cells.js 3000                        # on Bun
node cli.js run bench/cells.js -- 3000         # on the 5 MB QuickJS runtime
node bench/startup.js                          # launch to first frame: Node, Bun and both executables
node bench/startup.js --svelte                 # the same for the Svelte app
tkinter: canvas frame cost (headless, any platform):
py bindings/python/bench/tk_canvas_bench.py 3000 all    # move 3,000 canvas items every frame
py bindings/python/bench/tk_canvas_bench.py 3000 one    # move one
Inside any app: run it with BUI_PROFILE=1 to print per-phase frame times
(layout, paint, raster, present) every 60 frames; any value turns it on. Use
BUI_GPU=1 / BUI_GPU=0 to pick the renderer. More:
Profiling.
Works means it works and is tested. Experimental means it's written but has had little hands-on testing on real hardware (macOS: two Apple Silicon Macs so far, plus CI).
macOS. The macOS window host is new: it's a port of Blender's Cocoa code
(GHOST). So far it has been checked by CI and tried by hand on two Apple Silicon
Macs: by Krish Kalaria, who reported issue #3 and fixed it in pull request #4, and by DanNoby (17/17 tests; issue #6 added a toolchain note to the guide). If you have another Mac, especially an Intel one, please try it and
tell us what happens: docs/macos-testing.md. Python
can still use the stdlib Tk window there (BUI_HOST=tk; this needs Python's
tkinter, for example from python.org or brew install python-tk). Node runs
BUI on its own UI thread and macOS only allows windows on the main thread, so
JavaScript stays headless on macOS for now.
Linux. libX11 and libGL are loaded when the first window opens, so BUI also
imports and renders headless on servers and in containers without them, and
falls back to the CPU raster where OpenGL is missing. Building from source needs
the X11 headers (libx11-dev / libX11-devel); no GL headers are needed. The
C, Python, window and GPU parity tests pass on Linux, on Mesa's software OpenGL
and on an NVIDIA GPU.
Packages:
Most are read by the C library, so they work the same from every language.
On/off variables look at the first character: 1, y, Y, t or T is on.
Where a variable and an app-wide API call set the same thing, the variable
wins.
Every variable, with defaults and where it's read: Environment variables and docs/getting-started.md.
You need CMake 3.20+, a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC/MinGW or Clang) and Python 3.11+ with headers. On Linux, also the X11 headers.
git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j 2
ctest --test-dir build                      # C, C++, ImGui and Python test suites
export PYTHONPATH=$PWD/bindings/python      # Windows: set PYTHONPATH=%CD%\bindings\python
python examples/components_demo.py
cd bindings/rust && cargo test              # Rust: CSS, Tailwind, rsx!, hooks, effects, headless windows
Rebuild the docs screenshots with python tools/gen_doc_images.py (and the
website's dark and light shots with --site). More:
CMake options.
How each was counted: Coverage, SYNTAX_COVERAGE.md, docs/rust.md, docs/imgui.md.
Known limitations. Read these before you pick BUI for something you will ship. The tables below have the details.
- No accessibility support. BUI draws its own widgets and does not talk to the platform's accessibility APIs (UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS), so screen readers can't see them. Don't use it for software that has to be accessible. Accessibility is planned.
- Text. Blender's bundled Inter font only (system fonts only with the Windows GDI option). No per-glyph font fallback (missing characters show as boxes), no input methods (IME), right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, and no OpenType features.
- It doesn't look native. BUI looks like Blender: its Dark and Light themes (other Blender theme files can't be loaded yet). It doesn't follow your operating system's theme, accent color or fonts.
- Rendering. The CPU rasterizer is the default and works everywhere. The optional GPU renderer is Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL 3.3 on Linux. There is none on macOS (no Metal): macOS always draws on the CPU. Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends don't exist yet.
- Platforms. Windows and Linux (X11; Wayland through XWayland) are the supported ones. macOS is experimental: checked by CI and tried by hand on two Apple Silicon Macs, and JavaScript windows are headless there. The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 only.
- Retained mode, no visual editor. BUI keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI; it is not an immediate-mode library. There is no drag-and-drop UI designer: you write the UI in code.
- Performance numbers come from one machine, a Windows 11 laptop (Ryzen 7 5800U). Linux and macOS haven't been measured yet.
- The home page demos are browser sketches, not the native engine (the page says so). Run the Python, Rust or JavaScript examples to feel the real widgets. A WebAssembly build is planned.
- It's a port, not Blender unchanged. Widget drawing and interaction are
ported from Blender's UI sources, with edits (each marked BUI:), and the rest
of Blender (its data system, window manager and operators) isn't included.
There is no automated sync with Blender's releases.
- Partial areas: Qt syntax (about 24%), CSS (261 of 745 properties render), video has no audio, and image formats such as AVIF, EXR, TIFF, JPEG XL and HEIC aren't supported.
- License. GPL: a program that includes BUI is distributed under the GPL too (why).
Done
Partial or in progress
Planned (coming soon)
Our roadmap has no dates on it. Like a good render, it's done when the noise goes away.
Do I need Blender installed?
No. BUI contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own.
Is it really my unchanged tkinter app?
Yes.blenderui-tk app.py makes import tkinter return BUI's
implementation, which covers every public tkinter and ttk name. Nine real
programs are tested to behave identically on the standard library and on BUI.
See the limitations for the few
differences.
Is it a web browser in Rust?
No. There's no browser engine and no network. BUI takes HTML elements and CSS as a UI language: they are laid out with taffy and drawn by BUI's engine, with Blender's widgets where you ask for them, in a native window. JavaScript is optional: the Rust crate needs none, and the JavaScript packages drive the same engine.
Is the Dear ImGui support a re-implementation?
No. It's the real Dear ImGui (vendored, MIT), running on a BUI backend, so every function behaves as upstream. The optional Blender-widgets build swaps only how ImGui's widgets are drawn and how they react to the mouse, by compiling an edited copy ofimgui_widgets.cpp.
How is it different from Electron, Electrobun or GPUIX?
- Electron ships Chromium with every app: on the order of 100 MB or more.
- Electrobun runs on Bun and renders in the system's webview. It's small to download, but the UI is still a browser page.
- GPUIX, like BUI, renders React natively: React drives Zed's GPUI.
BUI also renders natively, with Blender's widgets, a much larger part of CSS, Tailwind, and hooks backed by signals.
bui build makes a 5 MB
executable that reaches its first frame in about 70 ms.
Do the macros cost performance?
rsx!, #[component], css! and tw!
expand at compile time into the same builder calls you would write by hand.
Tailwind classes are compiled to CSS once, on first use. Hooks are a few
nanoseconds per read or write.
Can I change the colors?
Yes. Switch between Blender's Dark and Light themes at run time (Themes), color individual widgets in every API, and use full CSS on plain HTML elements in Rust and JavaScript. Loading any other Blender theme file is coming soon.
Does it run on my Mac?
Probably, but nobody has checked yet: the Cocoa host is written and experimental. Python can always fall back to the Tk window (BUI_HOST=tk). If you try it, the notes in
docs/macos-testing.md say what to report.
Is it ready for production?
Much of it is complete and tested (the C kit, tkinter, the components, Rust, Dear ImGui, JavaScript), and some parts are partial or experimental (Qt syntax, parts of CSS and text, macOS). Status and roadmap shows which is which. Pin your version, and test on the platforms you ship.
Who wrote it?
All of the code was written by LLM coding agents. None was typed by hand. A human directs the work, sets the rules the agents follow (`AGENTS.md`) and reviews the results.
The method matters. Instead of asking an agent to write a UI toolkit from scratch, the maintainer started from Blender's own UI sources and asked it to remove everything that isn't UI logic. Agents are much more reliable at removing than at generating, and what stays is Blender's code. The drawing and interaction code is ported from Blender's sources, and the behavior is checked by tests: C, Python, Rust and JavaScript suites, the tkinter side-by-side programs and the GPU parity test.
Why GPL?
BUI is derived from Blender's source code, so it follows Blender's licensing: the whole is under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later, and individual files keep their own compatible license (`GPL-2.0-or-later` for the files that come from Blender).
Is it immediate mode? Is there a visual UI editor?
BUI is retained-mode: it keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI, and redraws only what changed. There is no visual UI editor yet; you write the UI in code (tkinter, Qt-style, Blender components, Rust, JavaScript or C).
Is the C API stable?
Not before 1.0, but it is versioned:BUI_kit.h has BUI_KIT_VERSION_* macros
and BK_version() reports the library's version, the same number as the Python, Rust and
npm packages. Every change that breaks existing code is listed under "C API changes" in the
changelog. Pin a release number, not a commit. From 1.0 it follows semantic versioning
(details).
Is BUI accessible to screen readers?
Not yet. See the known limitations.
Can I use BUI in a commercial app?
The GPL allows commercial use. What it asks is that when you distribute a program that includes BUI, you distribute it under the GPL too, with its source code available. If that doesn't fit your project, talk to a lawyer before you ship. (This is a summary, not legal advice.)
Contributions are welcome: bug reports, missing tkinter/Qt behavior, CSS features, platform hosts and docs. If you have a Mac, running the Cocoa host and reporting what happens is one of the most useful things you can do right now. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, and please follow the Code of Conduct. Report security issues privately, as SECURITY.md describes.
Releases go to PyPI (blenderui, wheels built by CI on a v* tag), crates.io
(the eight Rust crates, in dependency order) and npm (@blender-ui/native, @blender-ui/react). The steps are
in docs/publishing.md.
License. BUI follows Blender's licensing. BUI as a whole is licensed under
the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (the text is in
LICENSE). Individual files may have a different, but compatible license: the
files that come from Blender keep Blender's SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header, and new files carry the same one. Third-party parts
keep their own licenses:
The Rust and JavaScript bindings also depend on crates and packages such as taffy, napi-rs, React and QuickJS, each under its own license.
The full license texts of everything above, and of every Rust crate BUI's packages are
built from, are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. It ships inside the
Python wheels, the npm packages and the crates, and python tools/gen_notices.py regenerates it.
Acknowledgments. Thank you to:
- Blender and its community: the UI this project is built from, including its GHOST window code and blenlib.
- Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut: the immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI.
- taffy: flexbox, grid and block layout for the Rust crate.
- Tailwind CSS: the v4 theme behind the Tailwind support.
- FreeType: glyph rendering, as in Blender.
- stb_truetype: font metrics and the fallback rasterizer.
- NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen: the icon rasterizer, via Blender's edited copy.
- Inter by Rasmus Andersson: the embedded UI font, as in Blender.
- Slug by Eric Lengyel: the GPU glyph coverage algorithm.
- gpui, zopra and Leptos: the APIs the Rust syntax follows.
BUI is Blender's UI, minus the default cube. You're free to add your own.

At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
07:18:44 UTC
16:18:44 KST

At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since this summer to curb, restrict, or end their use of Flock Safety technology as concerns about mass surveillance and data privacy continue to grow. The backlash is part of a broader pushback against the rapid adoption of advanced AI technology, including the data center buildout, facial recognition, and other uses of AI.
Flock, founded in 2017, sells surveillance software that can help solve crimes, such as finding missing people or stolen cars. Its products include license plate readers, drones, and microphone-based edge-computing devices to pick up gunshots and other sounds. More than 100,000 Flock cameras are in use nationwide.
But in the past three months, Monroe, Ohio; Newburgh, New York; Richmond, Virginia; Hopkinton, Massachusetts; New Bedford, Massachusetts; and Lansing, Michigan, have all moved to end their contracts with Flock. Meanwhile, police in East Bridgewater and Grafton, Massachusetts, also announced plans to stop using Flock cameras. Just this week, residents of League City, Texas, voted against their police department’s continued use of Flock’s license plate readers, and the cameras are now set to be removed.
The concerns range from privacy to how data is shared (and with whom) to procurement concerns.
In Asheville, North Carolina, police lost access to Flock after the city voted to terminate its contract in August, and the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office in Colorado announced in September that it would stop using Flock cameras. When asked for comment, the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office redirected TechCrunch to its press release, where Sheriff Joseph Roybal said that discontinuing the use of Flock was the right decision for the county.
“We have the tools, training, and experience to locate and apprehend criminals without relying on Flock cameras,” he said in the press release.
Tatiana Rice, a senior director for U.S. legislation at The Future of Privacy Forum, told TechCrunch that the backlash to Flock isn’t surprising and only further represents the “growing public skepticism toward technology.” Flock is a target because people can see the sensors and cameras as they drive along roads; data centers have also become physical embodiments of the resentment growing against emerging technology. “A camera at the end of your street is tangible in a way that everyday sharing and selling of personal data online is not,” Rice said.
At the state level this summer, for example, Florida barred license plate readers from state highways, while Texas paused state funding for Flock. The issues again range from data privacy concerns to misuse of the technology.
Misuse has been a real problem. In August, for example, an officer in Brentwood, Missouri was accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his ex-wife during their divorce. In September, an officer from East Texas was sentenced to prison for using Flock to stalk his ex-girlfriend and her family.
Another growing concern is how immigration officials have been able to access the technology. One case that captures the issue came in March, when Ithaca, New York, passed a resolution to terminate its contract with the Flock Group.
In the resolution, the city said there were “proven instances of Flock Safety infrastructure being used by federal agents for information purposes even without specific authorizations from the contracting locality,” and that the city had reviewed reports that “either intentionally or through its negligence,” Flock had allowed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to “use query results from its database of state and local ALPR [automatic license plate reader] data to investigate and persecute immigrants throughout the United States.”
“Every day, police departments across the country are using Flock technology to solve serious crimes, locate suspects, find missing people, and make a measurable impact on public safety,” Flock told TechCrunch in a statement. “While we respect every community’s decision, removing a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes and protect communities moves public safety backward. Every Flock customer owns its data and controls who it is shared with and how it can be used. Flock does not sell data and does not have a contract with ICE.”
This August, Flock announced it would shorten the default period it stores data for new customers, from 30 days to seven. It also said agencies now need a case code before they can search the database.
The conversation around Flock echoes, in many ways, the fight over data centers. Many of these cities adopted Flock just a few years ago, and residents likely had no idea it was being installed, Adam Schwartz of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy nonprofit that has investigated Flock before, told TechCrunch.
That lack of awareness is similar to how data centers are popping up across the country, often before residents understand what is happening. Schwartz said police departments often decide to use Flock on their own, with little oversight from city councils. In South Windsor, Connecticut, according to local reports, Flock cameras went live last year without public warning or a vote. In October, the town voted to remove its Flock cameras.
“Grassroots activists across the country have been demanding that city councils exercise their procurement power to refuse to pay for ALPRs,” Schwartz said, referring to councils’ power to decide what the city buys. He added that activists have been fighting for years and that “many city councils are listening.”
The main argument for technology like Flock is that it helps combat crime and keep neighborhoods safe. And many local governments are not dropping Flock or similar technology; instead, they are adding restrictions on its use or looking for alternatives.
Cleveland, Ohio, for example, voted this summer to extend its contract with Flock, but has started restricting searches related to immigration. It has also limited access to the database to the Cleveland Police alone, cutting off the Northeast Ohio Regional Fusion Center, essentially a federal intelligence agency, which had initially been given access.
“They are used and needed for investigative purposes,” the city said when reached for comment. “The Department of Public Safety is currently reviewing responses to an RFP [request for proposals] that was sent out to other vendors that provide the same technology as Flock.”
But as with data centers, communities want more say in the trade-offs. “These tools can offer real public safety benefits, but communities are clearly interested in ensuring that those benefits are not at the cost of their civil liberties,” Rice said. Surveillance technology will likely remain a political hot topic, especially since Democrats now control Congress.
In September, President Donald Trump said he liked Flock’s technology “because of law enforcement,” even though a Reuters poll that same month found that more Americans dislike the technology than like it.
Also that month, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced a bill called the Flock-Off Act to bar the use of federal money to buy “Flock-style surveillance” and put other safeguards in place. In October, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), and Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) introduced the Ban Flock Act to end “the rise of AI-powered surveillance cameras.”

Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy AI agent security startup Clutch for $500M

Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security, a startup that secures AI agents’ access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus additional milestone-based payouts, according to a person familiar with the discussions.
Three-year-old Clutch was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire, according to our source. The startup is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That means the acquisition, if completed, would value Clutch at about 50 times its ARR, a standard way of pricing software companies.
Palo Alto Networks and Clutch Security did not respond to a request for comment. The Information was the first to report the acquisition discussions.
The high valuation is not an anomaly in a market increasingly focused on securing software against bad actors using AI to breach systems more easily. Upwind, a startup using AI to secure cloud infrastructure, recently turned down an acquisition offer from DataDog that valued it at roughly 40 times ARR, TechCrunch reported last week.
If the deal happens, it would be Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The cybersecurity giant has a history of buying innovation rather than building it in-house, and it has ramped up dealmaking this year in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks.
In September, Palo Alto Networks acquired Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks. The transaction valued Console at $500 million in stock and cash, TechCrunch reported. Other VC-backed companies that Palo Alto Networks has scooped up this year include NEA-backed Embrace, for $325 million; Chronosphere, an observability platform backed by Greylock and Lux Capital, for $2.95 billion; and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $231 million, according to regulatory filings.
Several of Clutch’s competitors have also been acquired. Cyera, a cybersecurity startup valued at $12 billion earlier this year, acquired Oasis Security, which, like Clutch, focuses on managing AI agents’ access to systems, for $1 billion. Meanwhile, Cisco bought Menlo Ventures-backed Astrix for roughly $400 million, Calcalist reported.
