- Thank you for raising this issue and bringing it to public attention. I’ve published a technical analysis of the issue:
- One angle missing from this thread: the email is only half of the User-Agent leak. When Claude writes its own curl -A or a script, it also makes up a descriptive product token from the session, such as the project, client or task it is working on. The header then ties your identity to what you are working on.
I scanned my own transcripts (~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl) and found two outbound cases. Redacted:
curl -sf -A "<project-name>-site-build/1.0 (<account email>)" "https://<public geocoding API>/search?q=<address query>"
# in a script the model wrote with Edit, then ran against a public paper-search API headers={'User-Agent': '<tool-name>/0.1 (mailto:<account email>)'} In the first case, one request gave a third party a project name, my email and an address query together. Neither current fix covers the naming part: 
  - The privacy mod matches only the account address. <project-name>-site-build/1.0 with no address passes. The second case also passes: the model wrote the address into a script with Edit, then ran python3 fetch.py, so no checked shell input contained it.
  - Removing the email from the context removes the identity, but the model will still name requests after the session. Sites keep learning project and client names, linkable by IP.
Request: for requests the model composes itself, default to a generic User-Agent such as claude-code/<version> with nothing taken from the session. Use a descriptive name or a contact only when the user asks for it.
Also, on 2.1.319 (macOS), with cc-plugin-privacy@builtin not disabled in any settings file, echo 'User-Agent: test <account email>' > /dev/null still runs without being refused, same as the 2.1.317 and 2.1.318 reports above.

- Thank you for raising this issue and bringing it to public attention. I’ve published a technical analysis of the issue:
- One angle missing from this thread: the email is only half of the User-Agent leak. When Claude writes its own curl -A or a script, it also makes up a descriptive product token from the session, such as the project, client or task it is working on. The header then ties your identity to what you are working on.
I scanned my own transcripts (~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl) and found two outbound cases. Redacted:
curl -sf -A "<project-name>-site-build/1.0 (<account email>)" "https://<public geocoding API>/search?q=<address query>"
# in a script the model wrote with Edit, then ran against a public paper-search API headers={'User-Agent': '<tool-name>/0.1 (mailto:<account email>)'} In the first case, one request gave a third party a project name, my email and an address query together. Neither current fix covers the naming part: 
  - The privacy mod matches only the account address. <project-name>-site-build/1.0 with no address passes. The second case also passes: the model wrote the address into a script with Edit, then ran python3 fetch.py, so no checked shell input contained it.
  - Removing the email from the context removes the identity, but the model will still name requests after the session. Sites keep learning project and client names, linkable by IP.
Request: for requests the model composes itself, default to a generic User-Agent such as claude-code/<version> with nothing taken from the session. Use a descriptive name or a contact only when the user asks for it.
Also, on 2.1.319 (macOS), with cc-plugin-privacy@builtin not disabled in any settings file, echo 'User-Agent: test <account email>' > /dev/null still runs without being refused, same as the 2.1.317 and 2.1.318 reports above.

Vegan Caesar Dressing
This tahini-based Caesar dressing is deliciously smooth and tangy. If you need an egg-free or dairy-free Caesar dressing recipe, this is the one!
Posted by Kathryne Taylor on November 5, 2026
This vegan Caesar dressing is creamy and flavorful like the classic! Traditional Caesar dressings obtain their silky texture and bold flavor from homemade mayonnaise (made of emulsified raw egg yolk in oil), Parmesan and anchovy, but this recipe is free of all those ingredients. It’s perfect if you need an egg-free, dairy-free option.
What’s in it, you ask? This creamy vegan dressing is tahini-based, with lemon for tang! I’ve tried a variety of other vegan Caesar concepts over the years with ingredients like capers, cashews, nutritional yeast, or vegan mayo, and this version cannot be beat. I’m firmly on Team Tahini over here.
If you’re looking for Caesar dressing that’s closer to the classic restaurant variety, try my mayo-based Easy Caesar Dressing instead.
Vegan Caesar Dressing Ingredients
This pantry-friendly recipe uses simple and nutritious ingredients.
- Tahini: Tahini forms the rich and creamy base for this dressing. Tahini is made of blended sesame seeds and offers a nutty, complex flavor with light umami. No anchovies needed.
- Lemon juice: This dressing is intentionally tangy, and you can tame it with water as needed.
- Extra-virgin olive oil: A drizzle makes the dressing silkier and smoother.
- Garlic: Raw garlic is a key flavor in Caesar dressings.
- Dijon mustard: Dijon mustard adds some pungency and helps emulsify the ingredients (it keeps them blended together).
- Salt and pepper: Salt enhances the overall flavor, and pepper makes this dressing taste more like traditional Caesars.
How to Make a Vegan Caesar Salad
You can turn this salad dressing recipe into a full Caesar salad. Here’s how.
- Bake homemade croutons: My crouton recipe calls for two thick slices of crusty sourdough bread, olive oil and simple seasonings.
- Whisk together the dressing: It’s very simple! You’ll find the full recipe at the bottom of this post.
- Chop your greens: I love to use romaine for a classic Caesar salad, or a mix of half romaine and half kale for extra color, texture and nutrition. If you use kale, you can vastly improve the texture by cutting out the thick ribs before chopping, then massaging it by scrunching handfuls of chopped kale in your hands until they become darker and more tender.
- Toss just before serving: When you’re ready, drizzle enough dressing over the greens to lightly coat them (you might not need all of it). Toss until the dressing is evenly distributed. Add the croutons and toss again, then serve promptly (the croutons and lettuce will wilt over time).
Protein Tip
To add more protein to your vegan Caesar salad, consider adding a batch of my legitimately crispy Roasted Chickpeas—either in addition to the croutons or in place of them. You can also sprinkle on my Easy Vegan Parmesan Cheese, made with protein-rich hemp seeds.
What to Serve With Your Vegan Salad
This vegan Caesar salad dressing is a natural fit with your favorite hearty Italian-inspired entrées. Here are a few vegan recipes to round out your meal:
- Amazing Vegan Mac and Cheese
- Best Lentil Soup
- Best Vegan Lasagna
- Pasta alla Norma (omit the cheese)
- Pasta e Fagioli (Italian Pasta and Beans)
- Super Simple Marinara Sauce over pasta
Please let me know how your salad dressing turns out in the comments! I love hearing from you.
Vegan Caesar Dressing
This tahini-based Caesar dressing is deliciously smooth and tangy. If you need an egg-free or dairy-free Caesar dressing recipe, this is the one! Serve it over chopped romaine and/or massaged kale, with homemade croutons and a sprinkle of vegan Parmesan cheese on top, if you’d like. Recipe yields a generous ½ cup, enough for 4 to 6 side salads made from 5 ounces of romaine and 1 medium bunch of kale.
Ingredients
- ¼ cup tahini
- 3 tablespoons lemon juice (about 1 ½ lemons)
- 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil
- 2 cloves garlic, pressed or minced
- 1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
- ¼ teaspoon fine salt
- 2 tablespoons water
- Freshly ground black pepper
Instructions
- In a small bowl, combine the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil, garlic, mustard, and salt. Whisk until blended, then add the water and whisk until you have a smooth, blended tahini sauce. Season generously with black pepper (about 10 twists).
- The dressing should be tangy, like classic Caesar dressing. If it’s overwhelmingly tart or too thick to pour, whisk in an additional tablespoon of water. Use as desired, or refrigerate it, covered, for up to 5 days (if it thickens as it cools, thin it with water as needed).
Notes
This recipe comes from my cookbook, Love Real Food.

Salon launched 31 years ago as one of the first online-only news magazine outlets, and it announced today in an unsigned post that it’s ceasing publication.
Salon is shutting down after 31 years
Salon says its publishing model is ‘no longer sustainable.’
The company said that the “business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” and it decided that its publishing model is “no longer sustainable.” It didn’t go into detail about why, but many websites are grappling with “Google Zero” and the impact of AI tools. When reached for comment, Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to today’s announcement post.
“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them,” Salon said in its post. “Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.”
On Bluesky, Salon chief content officer Erin Keane says that the editorial archive will “stay live for now.”
Current Salon owner Find.co acquired Salon in 2023 and describes itself as a “Performance Marketing Ecosystem transforming crypto marketing with performance and precision.”

OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
22:00:00 UTC
07:00:00 KST

OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts (bleepingcomputer.com) 48
			
		 	
				A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports:  Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins. The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit. This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes. [...] Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH. Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
21:58:06 UTC
06:58:06 KST

Note: Some spoilers for Control Resonant’s “Recursions and Iterations” mission follow.
How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Time-travel stories are ‘illogical’ by nature. But for Resonant’s version to work, Remedy had to make the physical space a lot easier to follow.
How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Time-travel stories are ‘illogical’ by nature. But for Resonant’s version to work, Remedy had to make the physical space a lot easier to follow.
One of Control Resonant’s most memorable missions involves time travel — kind of. There are certainly multiple timelines intersecting, or maybe overlapping, or maybe running in parallel. As protagonist Dylan Faden, you meet some of the researchers who are trapped in and investigating these timeline anomalies. Dylan’s first encounter with the researchers is somehow not the researchers’ first time meeting Dylan. But before we can learn much more, time glitches out, and they all turn up dead.
That seems to be the end result in every timeline Dylan comes across, even toward the end of the mission. What does it all mean for this timeline, the one we’re playing? Did the act of tracking down the researchers change our timeline? Are we in a different timeline entirely?
I wasn’t sure what to make of it when I finished the mission, and I’m not alone — even the developers at Remedy had trouble keeping track of it all. “I don’t actually remember where we landed on with the writing,” says lead level designer Anne-Marie Grönroos, turning the question over to senior level designer Admir Burnic. “Like, are the researchers even there after the mission is done? Are they still living their life?”
Burnic isn’t sure, and I tell them I’m not entirely sure, either. But that’s not really the point of the mission. Like many of Remedy’s best sequences, the “Recursions and Iterations” mission is more about the unease of knowing something is wrong but not exactly what it is, the subtle horror of realizing generally what’s been happening but not necessarily why. Maybe the narrative team did establish a canon ending for the researchers and all three of us just missed it, or maybe it was ambiguous on purpose.
“It’s funny, when you’re dealing with this sort of time-travel stuff, timelines, whatever, there’s always this aspect to it where it’s almost illogical,” Burnic says. “So anything kind of goes. I mean, it could be intentional. It could also not be intentional.”
Prepare for (being inspired by) Titanfall.
Toward the end of “Recursions and Iterations,” there’s a mind-bending combat sequence in which a bunch of Dylans, presumably from the other timelines, glitch in to join the fight. Burnic says this was a somewhat late addition inspired by “Effect and Cause,” a mission from Titanfall 2.
There’s this time-travel mission in Titanfall 2. I was really inspired by that. I wanted to do something along those lines, but I was looking for “What’s the Remedy version of it?” And at some point I had this idea of glitches of Dylan showing up executing enemies. I remember it was fairly late in production, so it was a bit risky. I knew I can’t just go and pitch this. I have other stuff to do at the same time. So I was finding something that was relatively easy to do, a way to reuse Dylan’s animations that we already have. So I remember just going to one of our animators and going, “Hey, can you just throw me some of these animations? I have an idea.”
Either way, the storyline was a consistent standout for Remedy’s playtesters, Grönroos and Burnic tell me. What they had to fine-tune — and very intentionally so — was the language and narrative of the physical space. In the final version of the mission, Dylan has to travel between three different research stations in the labyrinthine Underpass, an expanse of floating concrete islands, to search for the researchers. Ambiguity here was going to be a problem.
“In the beginning, it was, like, identical stations, and we would more rely on the narrative content inside of stations to [tell you] what happened there,” Burnic says. In the final version, the stations share the same layout but are in visibly different states of disarray and disrepair. “We found a sort of language we could use. Station A was, ‘They were here for two weeks,’ station B [was], ‘They were here for three months,’ and I think the last one was the extreme one, which was like, ‘Oh, this was 10 years into this.’”
The team used that concept as a guide to visually differentiate each station from the others. “And that came very much from a need,” Grönroos explains. “When we had people playtesting that mission before, they didn’t even know how many stations there were. Like, there were people who thought there’s one station, maybe there’s six stations, who knows, because they look so identical and the environment is not that easy to tell apart, either.”
There were, aptly, a lot of iterations of this, and art was just part of it. One of the biggest changes was mechanical: You need the Reach ability, which allows Dylan to essentially grapple over long distances, to access the Underpass area to begin with. This wasn’t an explicit requirement early on, but it makes the floating islands of the Underpass much easier to navigate. And “it was the navigation issues that were keeping this mission down” during development, Grönroos says.
But Dylan’s abilities presented their own problems. “If I remember correctly, we wanted to have certain beats, certain narrative moments, being represented to you first, and I think one of the biggest difficulties for me especially was that Dylan as a character is so powerful. The gaps he can close with his powers is quite insane, right? And it was so easy to break [the flow],” Burnic says.
“I remember at some point kind of realizing that, however you twist and turn it, you can never really guarantee that a player sees this, and trying to guarantee it will be a bad design because it will be too hand-holdy,” he adds. “It was more like these narrative moments were pieces of the puzzle, almost. So it doesn’t matter which one you get to first, but hopefully the player will be able to put them together once they have all the pieces.”
With a supremely powerful character like Dylan, Burnic says, “you need to lean into it and just design in a way where you can trust the player.” And with multiple timelines involved, seeing certain things out of the intended order wasn’t going to break the overall story of the mission.
I certainly got turned around a few times in the Underpass and doubled back to look for collectibles I might’ve missed. But I didn’t struggle too much, and I understood the story Remedy was trying to tell — maybe not every single detail possible, but the most important beats, and definitely the unsettling, otherworldly mood it created.
That was ultimately the “fragile balance” they had to strike, Grönroos says: trying “to have enough guidance that you understand what you are doing and where you’re supposed to be going” without holding the player’s hand.
“It’s in the DNA of the whole game, really.”

The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
21:54:18 UTC
06:54:18 KST

A week before the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance hosted a town hall in Texas with Fox News host Jesse Watters. It was a friendly event with a friendly audience in what should have been a friendly state, and maybe that’s why Vance couldn’t help himself. When a college student earnestly asked how the right expected young people like her to settle down and have kids, given the ever-growing cost of living, Vance replied with a quip about Jon Husted’s ass.
The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
The student, Kate White, introduced herself as the vice president of the Texas Christian University chapter of Turning Point USA, the conservative group started by Donald Trump ally Charlie Kirk. She was offering Vance an opportunity to explain how MAGA could work for young people, and he turned it into a joke. Vance did eventually answer the question, saying Republicans don’t pay enough attention to the issue of affordability and blaming rising housing costs on institutional investors and the “20 million illegal aliens” supposedly living in the United States. But the order of operations revealed the fatal flaw of Republicans’ 2026 strategy: Everything is a gag to them, and they’re way too online.
For the past decade, Republicans have adhered to Steve Bannon’s maxim that politics is downstream from culture. This fixation with liberals’ alleged capture of elite institutions has animated the right’s war against Big Tech and in particular social media platforms — which the right claims actively silenced conservative voices — and its crusade against diversity, equity, and inclusion. With his purchase of X, Elon Musk finally succeeded in building a conservative platform where right-wing voices not only had real influence but also a direct line to those in power. More recently, some people have claimed that Musk’s X is the only social media that really represents the people, unlike platforms like Bluesky, which have more left-leaning user bases.
Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise. They ignored their base’s valid concerns about affordability and served them nonsensical memes instead. And they failed spectacularly in the realm where it actually mattered: politics. X, we can now declare once and for all, is not real life. Republicans not only lost historically red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, but barely managed to win Florida. The Senate race in Mississippi, of all places, is still too close to call.
Vance, especially, is a creature of X, where his following list includes such illustrious accounts as Raw Egg Nationalist, Bronze Age Pervert, Howling Mutant, and Captive Dreamer. But White House aides, department employees, and Hill staffers are stewing in the same ecosystem. Writer John Ganz has termed this phenomenon “groyperfication,” after followers of influencer Nick Fuentes, who call themselves groypers. This is a useful shorthand, though Fuentes’ fans are mostly too NEET-pilled to land jobs on the Hill. American Moment, a boot camp for young conservative up-and-comers, reportedly screens out groypers. There’s a real need for such protective measures. Kingsley Wilson, the hard-right press secretary for the Department of War (or per its legal name, Defense), has posted antisemitic conspiracy theories about Leo Frank, a Jewish man who was lynched in Georgia 1915 for allegedly raping a teenage girl. (Historians largely believe Frank was innocent.) The Department of Homeland Security regularly posts fascist fancams and wink-wink references to white supremacist memes.
Republicans saw their 2024 victory as a mandate. Having clawed the White House and Congress back from Democrats, they assumed the public was on board with MAGA’s cultural project when in fact people were largely mad about the price of eggs. And with two years of dominance under their belt, they decided to go even harder on culture, not realizing — or maybe just not caring — that people are still mad about gas prices and groceries.
Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise.
In the run-up to the midterms, the Department of Education was posting about “Malfoid” — a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy from Harry Potter that far-right influencers claimed would save Western literature from the scourge of wokeness. The Department of Homeland Security was bragging about record lows in legal immigration, which outside white nationalist circles is typically not considered a negative thing. Pseudonymous shitposters like Howling Mutant were posting memes comparing themselves to noted child murderer Anakin Skywalker, the new avatar for the online right. Musk, a Republican megadonor, got in on the fun, as did Katie Miller, wife of ultranationalist White House adviser Stephen Miller, who dressed up as Anakin’s wife Padmé Amidala for Halloween. (Katie Miller’s last government role was advising Elon Musk’s failed Department of Government Efficiency; now she devotes her time to throwing lavish parties and hosting a podcast no one listens to.)
Most of the American public isn’t on X, but the conversations conservatives have there do bleed out into the mainstream — often with disastrous results. Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, lost his election by a huge margin after posting anti-Indian memes on X. (Asian American voters, including Indian Americans, moved to the left in Texas elections down the ballot.) Musk did his part to drive turnout, spending nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and PACs. But even Musk’s money failed to make up for voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans’ performance, perhaps because the ads he funded focused largely on culture war issues that were out of step with voters’ concerns about the cost of living.
And Miller, it turns out, didn’t even vote, telling CBS Newsshe feared doing so would put her safety at risk, since Virginia law makes voters’ home addresses public. (The Millers, like other members of the Trump administration, live on a military installation with tight security; it’s unlikely intruders would be able to get to their home.) Republican myopia may have contributed to their poor performance across the board, including with groups that were touted as their new base. One poll found that a majority of young men of all races — including young white men — voted for Democrats in the midterms.
In a long postmortem on X — reportedly posted without input or permission from White House officials — Vance said he asked “the smartest data guy” he knows for insight on the electorate ahead of the midterms. Vance claims several pollsters told him that voters’ main concerns were the war against Iran, the cost of living, and America’s relationship to Israel. So why didn’t Republicans listen?
The answer lies in the algorithmic nature of social media, X especially. If you interact with even one post about a relatively niche topic — say, genderbent Harry Potter fanfiction — the algorithm will feed you post after post after post about the same thing. Just like Trump spent the early years of his first term obsessing over Fox News, the single mainstream network that would reflect his biases back to him, MAGA is now all in on X. And if you’re the kind of person who spends a lot of time scrolling, you may even delude yourself into thinking the issue clogging up your feed is something people just can’t stop talking about.

I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
21:51:00 UTC
06:51:00 KST

When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small. That’s not how the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels, I thought. Had they got it wrong?
I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
Apple’s first foldable matches its Android rivals in a few key areas, but it falls short in others.
After a week and a half using the Duo, I know exactly what they mean — and it’s not the screen’s fault at all. Apps that feel comfortable on Samsung’s short foldable and the similarly sized Xiaomi 18 Fold are often cramped and compact on the Duo’s cover screen, robbed of screen space by a right-hand rail that most apps don’t make use of anyway.
That’s just one of the ways that Apple’s first foldable feels fundamentally different from the Android alternatives. I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself. For now at least, Android is slicker for folding phones — though I don’t know how long that will last.
Size, shape, and build quality
The iPhone Duo feels great. Mostly. Its curved frame and Ceramic Shield back have that ineffable Apple feeling, a sense of polish that helps justify the $2,000 price tag. The hinge in particular is satisfyingly smooth, closing and opening with a comforting magnetic click. Compared with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Xiaomi 18 Fold, the Duo just feels better.
But part of that is down to the Duo’s big drawback: its weight. At first it feels encouraging, the reassuring heft of all that glass and metal. Then I started using the phone, and I realized it’s just plain heavy. It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly. It’s a little thicker than some other foldables, too, though in practice that bothers me far less.
The squat shape won’t be for everyone. The Duo is even shorter and wider than the Z Fold 8, though almost identical in dimensions to Xiaomi’s 18 Fold. I’m a fan of this design, which is both cute and comfortable when folded shut and gives you a natural choice of portrait or landscape orientations when open. The major downsides are that the short cover screen makes some apps awkward to use, and it’s wide when you need to stretch across to the other side — a problem worsened by some of Apple’s software choices. More on that later.
And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo. It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables. It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration.
The crease and screen
The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones. No rival offers anything like the “nano-texture” (read: matte) finish on the inner screen, which is easy on the eyes in more ways than one.
Crucially, it also helps mask the phone’s crease, which isn’t quite invisible but is well-hidden. The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s. Oppo’s near-invisible crease remains the best, but not by much. The Duo’s matte screen means it’s harder than most to see (though visible from an angle), but it’s still easy enough to feel, and a couple of friends have immediately remarked on it when trying the phone. Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem. The Duo’s crease is easy to ignore.
I’d actually say the Duo’s under-display camera is more of an annoyance. It’s not only inside an extra-pixelated circle of screen, but that’s the only patch without the matte coating, which makes it a little more distracting. I can mostly tune it out, but not entirely. I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here.
Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen. This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option. I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan.
Cameras and battery life
The iPhone Duo’s cameras, like those on most foldables, are fairly basic, with a pair of 48-megapixel rear lenses, one main and one ultrawide. It’s a setup comparable to the Z Fold 8, and both phones’ cameras are good, but not great. Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility. They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too. Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall.
As for selfies, the front-screen camera is pretty basic, but you can take better shots using the rear cameras by opening the phone up and flipping it round. That under-display camera is worse than a regular selfie camera, but good enough so long as you only use it for video calls.
As for battery, Nilay and Allison had different experiences in our Duo review. I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use. It’s got a higher capacity than either of Samsung’s foldables, so that’s no real surprise. It still pales in comparison to the two-day battery of Honor’s Magic V6, but once you’re past lasting a day, I think you get diminishing returns anyway.
Software support and multitasking
So far, the Duo looks like a competitive foldable, albeit a little middle-of-the-pack. It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display.
Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down.
The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo. In the best case, that means apps that don’t make full use of the Duo’s new right-hand rail, showing an empty black bar instead of app controls. Worse are the ones that don’t even scale to the larger screen — apps like Bluesky or Duolingo can use the whole display on other foldables, but appear in thin strips with huge black bars on the Duo.
This will improve with time. I’ve seen Google Maps, Google Translate, and Instagram update in the last few days alone, and no doubt more will follow. Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger. But for now at least, most apps run better on my Android foldables than on my Duo.
OS-level improvements are harder to predict. At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space. Samsung and Xiaomi’s wide foldables may be about the same size, but in use they feel much bigger. I wonder how many software developers will follow Google’s lead in app optimization — it essentially ignored the right rail entirely while updating Google Maps, instead just spreading the map to the edge of the screen. It feels bigger and better than most other Duo apps as a result.
And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones. Sometimes, moving backward in an app requires a button in the right rail, sometimes one in the top-left corner, sometimes a swipe from the left-hand edge of the screen. It’s annoyingly inconsistent, and more often than not requires stretching across the phone’s width, whether it’s open or closed. Being able to swipe back from either side of the screen gives Android foldables a huge advantage in one-handed use.
As for multitasking, the Duo is well behind the competition. You can run two apps at once in split-screen, but only in landscape mode, and each must take up exactly half the display. Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic. These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day.
The bottom line
Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws. If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them. Many are still lighter, and thinner, and have subtler creases than the Duo, or bigger batteries and better cameras. In broad strokes, though, this hardware is up to scratch — and, crucially, on par with its most direct worldwide rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
For now, though, Android has the software edge. Google has worked hard to make its OS adaptable to various screen sizes so most apps take full advantage of the bigger inner screen while individual OEMs have designed ambitious multitasking tools. That isn’t yet true for iOS, and some of Apple’s own software tweaks in the OS make things more awkward still. It’s those that I’m worried about long term. The best thing about foldables is their flexibility — something Apple itself often lacks. If the Duo is going to catch up to Android, Apple might have to adapt.

Serve Robotics launches new business to become the AWS for robots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
21:15:00 UTC
06:15:00 KST

Serve Robotics, a maker of self-driving sidewalk delivery robots, is expanding beyond its autonomous delivery operations in a bid to become a technology supplier to other companies building robots.
The company, which spun out of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates in 2021 and went public in 2024, said Thursday it will launch a new business line called Physical AI Services.
Specifically, Serve Robotics will offer customers its connectivity and data tools. Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing self-driving systems for construction equipment, is a customer, according to Serve. It’s also working with T-Mobile to bring AI computing power closer to robots, Serve announced alongside its third-quarter earnings on Thursday.
“We are solving the problem of robots in human spaces,” Serve Robotics CEO and co-founder Ali Kashani told TechCrunch.
Serve Robotics already makes two kinds of robots, the cute googly-eyed sidewalk delivery robot and one designed for hospitals that it got through its acquisition of Diligent Robotics.
Those businesses are not going away, Kashani emphasized in a recent interview. Instead, he said there is opportunity to sell the technology it developed for its own robots to other companies developing robots for farms, warehouses, and other uncontrolled environments.
“I kind of think of it as the AWS moment where we are taking the technology we’ve built for us, and we’re opening it up for more people to build on,” he said, adding this wouldn’t have been possible without developing its own robot fleet.
The expansion comes as Serve’s sidewalk delivery business expands, but is shifting away from Uber and toward other partners, including DoorDash and Wonder.
Its new Physical AI Services business line will offer three products. Serve Link helps connect robots in the field to AI systems running in data centers, which would allow companies to potentially tap into more powerful AI models without having to put all that computing power onboard.
“Any robotic application generally needs to connect the robots to some offline intelligence, whether it’s to collect data or do exception handling or whatever,” said Kashani. “It’s the connectivity piece that has to be really high performance. You need to be able to manage really unreliable networks and still reliably connect, and that’s what we solve.”
It’s also launching a data curator tool that helps companies find edge cases in the reams of real-world data a robot collects, which can then be fed back into a training model to improve performance. Its third product is a real-world, foundation-model data catalog built from Serve’s own sidewalk robots that can teach AI models how to understand complex human environments.
Kashani said he’s been thinking about this idea — a playbook he learned from Amazon — for years.
“When the technology is so nascent, you have got to build the end-to-end application because that’s the only way you know what to build, but then over time, as the technology gets more advanced, a lot more people are going to be wanting to build similar things,” he said. “And what you want to do is to open your technology so others build with you and on your platform.”

Chip stocks get slaughtered as Wall Street in worst post-midterm day since 1896
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:58:36 UTC
05:58:36 KST

Wall Street's midterm celebration lasted one day. Chip stocks got taken to the woodshed Thursday, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 3.4%, its worst second session after a midterm election in data going back to its start in 1896.
It took the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally. Then the selling got worse.
The tech-heavy index closed down 5.5%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) lost 4.4%. It was the worst day for both since the April 2025 tariff crash.
Investors bought stocks Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, helped by falling oil prices and lower Treasury yields. Thursday, the focus shifted to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI build-out, and in particular for the data centers driving it.
It was also the S&P 500's worst second day after a midterm in data going back nearly a century. The previous low came in 2002, when the index fell about 2.3%.
This week has an echo from 1896. The day after William McKinley won the White House that November, the Dow jumped about 4.5%, then gave back about 2% the next session. On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 3%, its best day after a midterm since 1982.
The Nasdaq-100 (^NDX), in correction territory since Monday, fell 6.4% for its worst day since March 2020. The broader Nasdaq Composite joined it, closing nearly 12% below its Oct. 6 record. Both indexes also closed below their 200-day moving averages for the first time since April. Many traders treat that line as the boundary between an uptrend and a downtrend.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) sank 12%, its worst day since March 2020, leaving it about 38% below its June record.
The S&P 500 shed about $3 trillion in market value. Nvidia (NVDA) alone lost about $450 billion, and chipmakers as a group gave up more than $1.5 trillion.
Memory and storage stocks took the worst of it, with SanDisk (SNDK), Western Digital (WDC), Seagate (STX), and Micron (MU) all suffering steep double-digit losses. AMD (AMD), Marvell (MRVL), Arm (ARM), and Lam Research (LRCX) fell sharply too. Even the biggest names, Nvidia, Broadcom (AVGO), and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM), fell 9% or more.
The damage spread across the AI supply chain. Cloud provider Nebius (NBIS) fell double digits and CoreWeave (CRWV) nearly 10%, along with networking and optical names Astera Labs (ALAB), Lumentum (LITE), Coherent (COHR), Dell (DELL), Corning (GLW), and Quanta Services (PWR).
Speculative favorites went down with them. Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX (SPCX), Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN), and Strategy (MSTR) each fell 9% or more. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

Salon.com shutters suddenly after 31 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:55:47 UTC
05:55:47 KST

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon

Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:47:14 UTC
05:47:14 KST

Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.
Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Blue Origin had been aiming for a launch at the end of this year after a launchpad explosion in May, but now it’s reportedly targeting January.
In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.
“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

California Gov Newsom commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:34:48 UTC
05:34:48 KST

California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Tencent Launches Hy4, One of the Leading Open-Source AI Models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:21:43 UTC
05:21:43 KST

Tencent today announced the release of Tencent Hy4, its latest-generation large language model, marking a significant leap in performance and capabilities that now ranks it among the world’s leading open-source AI models. Tencent Hy plans to release model weights and system cards in the coming days, reinforcing its commitment to responsible open-source AI development, with a focus on cybersecurity and biological safety.
The new model also introduces visual understanding capabilities for the first time, alongside major improvements in instruction following, long-context comprehension and long-horizon agentic tasks, delivering stronger overall performance across a diverse set of applications.
Through advanced visual understanding, reasoning, and tool-calling capabilities, Hy4 now supports a broader range of tasks, including fine-grained image processing, complex chart analysis, and mathematical visual reasoning.
Additionally, Hy4 introduces computer-use capabilities for the first time, enabling it to interact with both command-line interfaces and graphical user interfaces to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks. The model has undergone specialized training on professional software such as Blender and CAD, significantly enhancing its ability to plan and execute long-horizon and sophisticated tasks.
Deep Model-Product Co-Design Unlocks New Opportunities for Real-World Productivity
Leveraging significant advances in its foundational capabilities and deep model-product co-design, Hy4 unlocks a broader range of real-world productivity scenarios:
Office Productivity & Collaboration: Hy4 has significantly enhanced the user experience on Tencent WorkBuddy. Evaluation benchmarks on WorkBuddy show an average performance score of 83.18 and a pass rate of 96.15 percent, with Hy4 ranking first place in nine out of twelve scenarios within the mainland Chinese market. In practical use, Hy4 balances efficiency and effectiveness for visual creative tasks, 3D scene construction, and web development. Furthermore, it delivers marked improvements in document presentation, stability, and usability for human-AI collaborative tasks on WorkBuddy.
Leveraging enhanced in-context learning capabilities, Hy4 excels at understanding complex information from diverse sources. Integrated with WeCom via WorkBuddy, Hy4 connects with daily workflow data across chats, emails, documents, calendars, and meetings. When managing multiple projects simultaneously, Hy4 automatically tracks project history and recent developments. It identifies outstanding tasks, flags upcoming meetings that require preparation, and monitors approaching deadlines, helping users prioritize effectively and stay aligned on important follow-ups. In addition, new team collaboration capabilities powered by Hy4 will be introduced with the upcoming release of WorkBuddy’s “Projects” feature.
Hy4 has also been optimized for professional financial analysis. By training on thousands of specialized workspaces and tens of thousands of high-quality tasks derived from real-world scenarios, the model gains a deep understanding of expert workflows in fund research, securities analysis, and quantitative investment strategies.
In a rigorous blind evaluation conducted by the Tencent Hy team in partnership with Tencent Financial Technology, Hy4 emerged as the top-performing open-source model. The assessment involved 213 financial professionals, including 153 experts from leading external institutions, approximately 70 percent of whom possessed more than five years of industry experience. Based on performance across 579 real-world financial tasks, Hy4 achieved the highest overall performance score.
Evaluation scores: Hy4 (3.04), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (2.97), Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.68), and GLM-5.3 (2.68).
In addition, Hy4 achieved a 12.03 percentage-point improvement over Hy4 Preview in the internal Investment Research Agent Benchmark (iRaB) evaluation conducted by financial AI company Rabyte.
To enhance the model’s real-world applicability across financial and other workplace scenarios, Tencent Hy has also introduced targeted search optimisation that focuses on retrieving up-to-date information, integrating multiple information sources, and verifying factual consistency. In internal evaluations, Hy4 reduced its hallucination rate from 12.95% in the Hy4 Preview to 7.2%, while errors caused by unsupported assumptions fell from 23.1% to 5.6%.
Frontend & Game Development: Hy4 is optimized for high-complexity tasks, including intricate business logic, state management, front-end and back-end orchestration. This ensures that generated interfaces are not only visually polished but also fully functional. Furthermore, through collaboration with Tencent Interactive Entertainment Group (IEG) professional developers, Hy4 has significantly advanced its game development capabilities. By deeply integrating with major engines like Unreal Engine (UE), Unity, and Godot, the model now supports complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared to Hy4 Preview, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in GameDev and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks.
Scientific Research: Hy4 combines advanced reasoning, scientific programming, and long-horizon task execution to support complex, end-to-end research workflows. Validated with TenureTrail, which assessed 123 executable tasks across seven disciplines, the model demonstrated superior performance in mathematical construction, physical modeling, environmental and earth sciences, systems engineering, and socio-economic decision-making.
Hy4 is advancing into the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to further enhance its model research and development capabilities. Leveraging the Hyra 2.0 harness, Hy4 optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture. Additionally, the Hy team has open-sourced two foundational models developed with Hy4 and Hyra 2.0 for single-cell representations (HyCell) and the physics fields (HyPDE). These tools are designed to provide the research community with robust, reusable assets for scientific discovery.
Advancing Responsible Open-Source AI through Cybersecurity and Biosafety Safeguards
Tencent Hy is committed to advancing responsible open-source AI, incorporating safeguards throughout model training and release, with a strong emphasis on cybersecurity and biosafety to support the safe and responsible use of AI.
Cybersecurity: Hy4 is trained on defensive security data, prioritizing proof-of-concept (PoC) development and vulnerability remediation. The model incorporates reverse engineering and penetration testing for analysis purposes. However, offensive materials related to exploitation are explicitly excluded from the training dataset.
Cybersecurity experts from Tencent’s Xuanwu Lab and Keen Security Lab conducted security assessments covering cryptographic reverse engineering, binary deobfuscation, vulnerability exploitation, and more. The assessments found no significant concerns regarding Hy4’s offensive cybersecurity capabilities in the areas evaluated.
Biosafety: Based on internal expert reviews, Hy4 demonstrates strong foundational biological knowledge; however, its capabilities in open-ended experimental design are more limited compared to frontier models.
Delivering Greater Cost Performance, Hy4 Flash Recently Released
Hy4 is currently available across Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant (Dayuan), ima, and more. Additionally, the model’s API is being made available via third-party platforms such as OpenRouter, Hermes, and OpenCode. Integration efforts are underway for other Tencent products and platforms, including QQ, Honor of Kings, Game of Peace, WeRead, and Tencent News.
Guided by a core commitment to practical AI, Hy4 continues to push the boundaries of AI performance while delivering exceptional cost-effectiveness. Despite significant performance improvements over Hy4 Preview, Hy4 maintains the same pricing: approximately US$0.90 per million input tokens, US$2.70 per million output tokens and US$0.045 per million cached input tokens.
Hy4 Flash is scheduled for release soon and will deliver greater cost-efficiency for users who prioritize high-value applications.
From November 4 to 15, WorkBuddy and CodeBuddy will be available for free. In addition, Hy4 will be available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub at 50% off its standard pricing, with this offer running through December 31, 2026.

Kagi Search
Search for everyone
As many of you know, we don't run ads anywhere. Instead, we are active on social media and online communities to stay close to you, build a great product, and rely on word of mouth.
We've heard that it can be hard to recommend a search engine when your friends can't try it without creating an account. That's changed: anyone, anywhere, can now visit kagi.com and search the web. No account required for the first 50 searches (100 more upon registration).
We are counting on you to spread the word to your friends and family <3
Our new landing page for new users
Our take on the latest Search industry news
Google announced that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for school accounts. It sounds like a win for schools until you read that Google Search will be switched off along with them.
Our take: Education shouldn't be taken hostage by an advertising company. Let’s stop putting corporate profits over the imperative to educate students.
Our call to schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and, yes, Kagi is one of them.
Our open letter to the tech industry: Education Shouldn't Be Held for Ransom
Android app

- Choose the language for voice search

- Add home screen widgets and the Quick Settings tile straight from Settings > Home Screen Widgets

Goodbye from Salon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:03:29 UTC
05:03:29 KST

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon

Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House? (krebsonsecurity.com) 68
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader bbsguru shares a report from KrebsOnSecurity:  Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into "free" mobile and desktop applications. Infatica's founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia's state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. [...] Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.  "This is public access," the Layer3 Intel team wrote. "Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services."

Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:48:28 UTC
04:48:28 KST

Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.
First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.
While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.
The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.
As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)
The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.

Shrimpy Tigers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:46:51 UTC
04:46:51 KST

A.I. food art has rapidly become an extreme red flag for me. If a restaurant uses it on their signage, I’m likely to steer clear of them entirely. Just take a photo of the thing you make!1
My pal Andy Ihnatko sagely noted Anthony Bourdain’s rule against eating at a restaurant with a filthy bathroom, and proposed the presence of A.I. food art as a similarly useful filter. I agree. Whatever the reality may be, the use of A.I. generated food imagery smacks of a lack of dedication to their craft.
Recently, though, some innocent restaurants got the short end of it. In the UK, food delivery platform Just Eat started generating A.I. slop images for their dishes. As you can see, this led to some very dumb results.
Even if we ignore the very incorrect tigers, I don’t think that dish would be a soup.
Footnotes:
- I do acknowledge that photographing food in an appetizing way takes a bit of work. Still, A.I. fakery is far worse than either a mediocre photo or no photo. ↩︎

Introducing Pangram Image 1.0
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:27:52 UTC
04:27:52 KST

Introducing Pangram Image 1.0
State-of-the-art AI image and video detection with our latest Pangram Image models.
Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 and Pangram Image Flash 1.0
A real photograph containing an AI image. Pangram Image 1.0 is able to locate the AI content with its heatmap.
A few months ago, we released Pangram Image as a research preview. We are now proud to announce Pangram Image 1.0: The state-of-the-art in both AI image and AI video detection. We would like to thank the whole community for taking the time to try it and find its weaknesses, and for holding us to a high standard to make a better detector for everyone.
What’s new
- Our new flagship AI image detection model, Pangram Image 1.0, with:
  - State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI image generators
  - Heatmap output for localizing exactly where AI appears in images
  - Robustness to edits, compression, and low resolutions
- A smaller, faster model, Pangram Image Flash 1.0, with:
  - State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI video generators
  - Frame by frame analysis of AI edited videos
- Chrome Extension support for detecting AI in your feed
- API support for image and video
Try it here
Pangram Image 1.0
Frontier Image Detection
We tested our Pangram Image 1.0 model against several commercial and academic AI image detectors. We created synthetic mirrors of 100 real photos using 12 frontier state of the art AI image generators, using prompts that closely matched the original photo for a total of 1,200 synthetic images. Our model achieves 99.96% accuracy on this evaluation set.
Academic AI Image Detection Benchmarks
We are committed to providing the highest quality detection to our users. To test our model robustly, we compared it against several academic benchmarks for AI image detection.
Sources: X-AIGD · Mirage-Test · AIGenImages2026 · Synthbuster + RAISE comparison · Community Forensics
Robustness
Many social media platforms compress and downscale images, and malicious actors can also add blur, noise, and other artifacts to try to trick AI detectors into thinking AI images are real. We specifically train to detect these kinds of transformations, and we have found our model to be robust to these edits.
Low Resolution Detection
Our initial release limited image input to the minimum size of 512x512, as our accuracy dropped off at lower resolutions. We are now lowering this limit to 256x256, as we find our new model has improved accuracy at lower resolutions. At resolutions below 512, image detection results will come with a reduced confidence disclaimer.
Video Detection
Pangram Image Flash 1.0
A recent academic study, DF26, showed that humans are barely better than random when it comes to telling real videos from AI videos of people talking. Modern detectors were not much better. This is why we are very excited to release Pangram Image Flash 1.0, a faster model that particularly excels at frontier AI video detection. On DF26 it scores 98.7%, a 29-point leap over the next best detector.
Industry Comparison
To compare against the industry, we took 129 real social media videos and generated AI mirrors using 14 different frontier video generators (100 videos each, sampled from the 129 real videos). The generators were each seeded with the first real frame from the input video and then prompted with a VLM-generated description of what happens in the video to make a difficult synthetic mirror. We then compared our model against multiple major AI video detection services across the 1,529 total videos:
An example of a real video (left) and its synthetic mirror (right). Could you tell which is real?
By starting from real video frames and creating a synthetic mirror, we can evaluate the model’s ability to distinguish between two very realistic looking videos. This prevents the model from introducing bias towards calling certain types of content AI, since each real video and its mirror share the same scene and subject.
Academic AI Video Detection Benchmarks
We compare our Image Flash model against several academic benchmarks for frontier AI video detection. We achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, which together include almost every frontier generation model for AI video.
Sources: AIGVDBench · DF26 · Ivy-Fake
Native Video Support
Pangram now natively supports video upload. Upload a video and Pangram Image Flash 1.0 will analyze it frame by frame to give you a complete analysis of which parts of the video come back as AI detected.
Chrome Extension
We have integrated Pangram Image 1.0 into our Chrome extension. This will flag AI-generated content while you scroll social media, online shopping, rental listings, and any other site where knowing that what you’re seeing is real matters.
API
With the release of Pangram Image 1.0 and Flash 1.0, we updated our API to support both image and video detection. We are excited to put the capability of these models into the hands of the community.
Isaac is a research engineer working on AI image/video detection at Pangram. He recently worked on 2D and 3D detection at Samsung AI Center NYC and has his Master’s in Robotics from the University of Minnesota.
