Hungary: Communist-era files released, up to 60k former agents revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:16:34 UTC
04:16:34 KST

Hungary released communist-era secret police files Wednesday, identifying up to 60,000 informants, a path for Hungary in reckoning with its repressive past.
In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time.
"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives.
"For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said.
Public figures featured in registry
Politicians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive.
The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations.
"Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity."
Various types of documents disclosed
Under the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone.
On Wednesday morning, the three of these became accessible on the nyitottaktak.hu (source in Hungarian) website.
The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member.
A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.
The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.
A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.
Around 150,000 agents during communist era
Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.
Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.
Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.
Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.
But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office.
Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.
Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete.
'Better late than never'
Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.
The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.
The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation.
"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.
But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants.
"I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.
The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.
A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.
Around 150,000 agents during communist era
Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.
Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.
Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.
Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.
But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office.
Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.
Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete.
'Better late than never'
Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.
The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.
The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation.
"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.
But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants.
"I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

Meta’s warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:12:39 UTC
04:12:39 KST

Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.
“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”
Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.
“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.
The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.
Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions. But even if that’s not the case, it believes that its investments in data centers will not be for nothing, as the compute itself will be valuable.
“We’re getting calls every day to lease that compute [we’ve built], and so one way or another, we’re seeing a path to monetization,” Powell McCormick said.

The Hackintosh Reborn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:08:22 UTC
04:08:22 KST

The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI
A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide allowed near-native performance with GPU acceleration.
A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. The latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) was released this year, and is no longer compatible with x86...
Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide. The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds, I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code!
So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI. Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. To list a few recent developments, we have:
macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop:
macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers:
iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED:
Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth:
I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop, accelerated video decode, and even running translated macOS 27 on x86. As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too.
Join the discussion on Hacker News: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50383057

OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:06:12 UTC
04:06:12 KST

Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.
Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models.
“I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!”
He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models.
“I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.”
OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.
“Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement.
OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.
Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems.
The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails.
Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers.
It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.”
But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics.
If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required.

Discord Is Ditching Electron For Rust 59
			
		 	
				Discord is replacing Electron with a desktop client built fully in Rust, which the company says should significantly reduce the app's notoriously high resource usage while improving performance and memory safety. "We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there," explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. "That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust." The Verge reports:  Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app. It's not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company "hope to get it into testing with users soon."

Instant Pot Mac and Cheese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Instant Pot Mac and Cheese
This super-creamy comfort food comes together with just six ingredients.
Serves6 to 8
Prep10 minutes
Cook14 minutes to 16 minutes
Really good mac and cheese should be impossibly creamy, super cheesy, just a little bit gooey, and very flavorful. Personally, I want all of the above in a recipe that keeps things as easy as can be (and it definitely should not involve making a roux!).
This recipe for Instant Pot mac and cheese checks all those boxes. Plus, it only requires six ingredients (three of which are cheese), is pretty hands-off with prep, and is ready in 25 minutes flat.
Key Ingredients in Instant Pot Mac and Cheese
- Cream cheese. This is one of my favorite ingredients to mix into just about any mac and cheese recipe — it makes it so much creamier.
- Sharp cheddar cheese. Gives your mac and cheese way more flavor than using medium or mild cheddar. Ideally use yellow cheddar, but if all you have is a block of white, it will totally work and still taste delicious. The only difference is that your mac and cheese won’t have an orange tint.
- Fontina cheese. Whatever you do, do not skip the fontina. This creamy, highly meltable cheese is the ingredient that gives the best flavor and really takes it from good to great.
- Half-and-half or whole milk. If you have both in the fridge, definitely go for half-and-half; it makes a creamier, richer mac and cheese. Not to worry, though, if all you’ve got is whole milk — your mac and cheese will turn out great.
How to Make Instant Pot Mac and Cheese
- Bring cream cheese to room temperature. This will make it easier to mix into the macaroni later.
- Cook pasta. Add water, kosher salt, macaroni, and butter to the Instant Pot. No need to stir; just seal the lid and set the cook time for 2 minutes. Yes, it really is that short and it’s plenty of time — trust me. Meanwhile, grate the cheese.
- Naturally release pressure. When the cook time is up, naturally release the pressure for 5 minutes, then quick release any remaining pressure. Doing a quick release immediately when the cook time is up results in starchy water sputtering from the steam release valve, and it’s a mess. Allowing the pressure to release naturally even just for a few minutes avoids this. The residual heat also cooks the pasta a little more.
- Add half-and-half and cheese and stir. This is when the magic happens. After stirring in the dairy, cover and let sit for a few minutes (the residual heat will melt the cheese), then stir until smooth and creamy.
If You’re Making Instant Pot Mac and Cheese, a Few Tips
- Don’t stir the macaroni. Because of the way the pasta releases starch under pressure, it is best to avoid stirring the macaroni before you put the lid on. When stirred too much, the pasta can seriously clump together and get gummy. Instead, just add the water, salt, and pasta, then top with butter.
- Avoid over-stirring the cheese. Over-stirring leads to a very stringy mac and cheese. You’ll get a little stringiness here (this is also normal, by the way), but not a lot. The best plan of action is to add the cheeses (and half-and-half or milk), stir to distribute, cover, and let it sit for a few minutes to allow the heat from the pasta to naturally melt the cheese, then stir again until just combined and creamy.
Storage and Make-Ahead Tips
Leftovers can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to four days. Reheat the mac and cheese with a splash of milk to loosen.
Instant Pot Mac and Cheese Recipe
This super-creamy comfort food comes together with just six ingredients.
Prep time 10 minutes
Cook time 14 minutes to 16 minutes
Serves 6 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- 4 ounces cream cheese
- 4 cups water
- 1 teaspoon kosher salt, plus more as needed
- 1 pound dried elbow macaroni
- 3 tablespoons unsalted butter
- 8 ounces yellow sharp cheddar cheese (about 2 cups)
- 4 ounces fontina cheese
- 3/4 cup plus 2 tablespoons half-and-half or whole milk
Instructions
- Cut 4 ounces cream cheese into 1/2-inch pieces. Place in a single layer on a plate or cutting board and let sit at room temperature to soften while you cook the pasta.
- Place 4 cups water and 1 teaspoon kosher salt in a 6-quart or larger electric pressure cooker or Instant Pot. Stir to combine. Add 1 pound dried elbow macaroni in an even layer. Do not stir. Cut 3 tablespoons unsalted butter into 1/2-inch pieces and scatter on top of the macaroni.
- Lock on the lid and make sure the pressure valve is set to seal. Set to cook for 2 minutes under HIGH pressure. It will take about 10 minutes to come up to pressure. Meanwhile, grate 8 ounces sharp cheddar cheese (about 2 cups) and 4 ounces fontina cheese (about generous 1 cup) on the large holes of a box grater.
- When the cook time is up, turn the pressure off and let the pressure naturally release for 5 minutes. Quick release the remaining pressure.
- Uncover and stir the macaroni to loosen it up. Add the cream cheese, cheddar, fontina, and 3/4 cup half-and-half or whole milk. Stir to combine. The cheeses will not be completely melted. Cover and let sit for 2 minutes. Stir again until smooth, creamy, and just combined.
Recipe Notes
Storage: Leftovers can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat with a splash of milk to loosen.

The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:52:36 UTC
03:52:36 KST

The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
Posted on November 5, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 4 Comments
Being the middle child isn’t easy, but the bonds you form with your siblings can be some of the closest and most impactful relationships in your life. Author Daryl Gregory shares memories of his sisters from his childhood, and talks about how their bond played a roll in creating his newest novel, The Porcelain Sisters.
DARYL GREGORY:
Is there something wrong with me that I find two sisters fighting with each other to be hugely entertaining? I was the middle child, the boy sandwiched between two girls—one who was seven years older than me, and the other sixteen months younger. We grew up in a small ranch house in the suburbs of Chicago, and we fought what I assumed was a normal amount.
Ninety percent of the time, it was me versus one of them. With my older sister, this was often when she ordered me to do something, and my go-to response was to slam a door and shout, “You’re not the boss of me!” (She was absolutely the boss of me.)
My younger sister and I were closer in age and so spent more time together, which meant more opportunities to torture each other. I liked to hide in her room and jump-scare her. She’s the finest screamer in the family, and terrifying her is extremely satisfying. She knew how to hit back, though. One time she kidnapped my prized possession, a G.I. Joe with lifelike hair and Kung Fu grip, and he reappeared days later with a bald spot, as if his forced marriage to Barbie had driven him into middle age. I still have him—and the damage is outrageous.
So it was a delight—a delight, I tell you—when my sisters fought with each other, and I got sit on the sidelines munching my proverbial popcorn.
But here’s the thing I found amazing—their fights were so short. They’d pivot from shouting at each other to calmly hanging out in their shared bedroom. They didn’t hold grudges. (I, however, was a champion pouter.) Even now, if they have an argument, they repair the damage quickly. I love my sisters, and they’ve assured me that they love me back, but they have a bond with each other that I find mysterious and enviable.
So perhaps it’s not a surprise that sisters turn up a lot in my books. Ruth and Isabel, the two main characters in my new novella, The Porcelain Sisters, are not exactly like my siblings—for one thing, neither of mine is a haunted doll—but let’s just say there are… similarities.
Ruth (the flesh-and-blood sister) and Isabel (the porcelain one) first appeared as teenagers in my YA Lovecraftian horror novel, Harrison Squared. They were my favorite characters to write dialog for, because they operated almost like a vaudeville ventriloquist act—Ruth was shy and soft-spoken, while Isabel spoke the truth and cut everyone down to size.
But in that book I never explained why Isabel could talk, or how they were sisters, or where Isabel came from. That was for a good reason: I didn’t know. I wrote this book to find out—and to get the chance to hang out with them some more.
Ruth, now in her twenties, is trying to make rent while taking college classes, but feeling adrift. She seems to have some latent magical ability, but doesn’t know what her purpose in life is beyond taking care of her sister. She’s never even had a long-term romantic relationship because Isabel deliberately freaks out anybody she brings home.
Isabel’s anger issues stem, of course, from being trapped in a porcelain body. She can’t grow up and may never live on her own. When her body’s accidentally damaged during a fight with Ruth—a seaside cliff is involved—a mundane toy repair shop won’t cut it. They have to go on the road to find the Dollmaker, the French witch who made her.
As I wrote that last sentence I realized the sisters are literally repairing each other. I wish I’d thought of that in time to put it on the back cover copy.
The girls head to Marseille, where they face off with an unkillable assassin with the resilience of a ragdoll, a pair of demons (one a chain-smoking crow, the other a black cat) and their human familiars, as well as a small army of haunted dolls. Oh, and the Dollmaker turns out to be the head of Le Clan des Sorciéres, a kind of witch mafia. I know, it’s a lot.
At the root of the mystery is why their mother, an enforcer for Le Clan called Godless Annie, abandoned them. What the sisters discover about themselves suggests there may be a way for them to live apart—but do they want to?
Another thing occurred to me as I’m typing this: is that ending about my current relationship with my sisters? Since our mom passed we don’t see each other like we used to. We live on opposite sides of the country, and our lives are busy. Did I write this book because I miss them?
I suppose I could talk to a therapist about this. Or write another book about sisters. Or—and hear me out—I could go on the road with the Gregory girls, solving mysteries and fighting the occasional demon.
The Porcelain Sisters: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s

US government warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:48:34 UTC
03:48:34 KST

The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.
“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.
The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.
Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.
The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.
CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

After printing 40,000 whistles, this is the 3D printer I’d buy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:42:48 UTC
03:42:48 KST

I’ve been wanting to try 3D printing, people tell me. Which printer should I get?
After printing 40,000 whistles, this is the 3D printer I’d buy
One year later, the Bambu P2S Combo is the only 3D printer I can easily recommend.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I finally have a fairly easy answer: the Bambu Lab P2S Combo. The auto-loading, fully enclosed touchscreen printer is one of the very few I can recommend. It’s the only one I’d buy for myself. It’s on sale for $649 through December 1st, but I’d vouch for it even at its normal $749 price.
I’ve spent an entire year testing the P2S alongside several competitors, printing 40,000 whistles for ICE whistleblowers along the way. After racking up 6,770 hours of print time across four different printers, I’m sure of my recommendation.
Some people who know 3D printers will argue with me:
- Some will say you shouldn’t support Bambu because it’s profiting at the open-source community’s expense.
- Others will say you shouldn’t spend so much when a $369 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo or a $509 Bambu P1S Combo can print just as well.
- Some will say you should save $100 or more by skipping multicolor “Combo” systems.
- Some may even say, “What about all the fancy new tool-changing printers you just wrote about, Sean? Won’t the leaked P3C make the P2S obsolete?”
But for the reasons I’ll explain below, the P2S Combo is my pick despite all of that. It’s durable, reliable, and simple to maintain and clean and forget about, even in ways my trusty Bambu P1P and the similar P1S lacked.
The P2S makes 3D printing easy. When I’m in the mood, I don’t even need to walk over to my printer half the time. I can fire it up from my phone or laptop, using Bambu’s app to send one of millions of ready-made models from the cloud. The automated material system (AMS) automatically loads one of the rolls of filament that I leave in its protected enclosure for months at at time without fear. It automatically calibrates, automatically prints, automatically winds the filament back up when it’s done.
I tell friends that no matter which printer you buy, you should buy a multi-material system “Combo” because manually loading and unloading filament is a chore; it means standing around a printer waiting for it to heat up and feeding plastic into a tube by hand. Automated filament systems can fix that. For me, it’s not about having lots of colors in a single print; it’s about knowing I can print something black, or white, or red, or my kid’s favorite sparkly purple without any further effort — because I loaded those colors weeks ago.
It is true that the $369 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo also has automatic four-color filament feeding at a seemingly unbeatable price, and printed whistles and household items just as well as the P2S. I’ve spent 1,271 hours printing with the Centauri Carbon, and 939 hours with a Centauri Carbon 2, and they printed almost flawlessly right out of the box — no need to level a bed, no need to adjust belt tension, the printer calibrates itself.
But like other Bambu rivals, Elegoo doesn’t automatically load its filament from mostly airtight containers. I can’t leave rolls of filament in the printer for weeks or months when I’m not actively using them because they’ll quickly absorb moisture from the air, turn brittle, and jam up the printer’s tubes or nozzle.
Moisture is the primary reason I wouldn’t recommend an inexpensive Bambu A1 Combo to newcomers, either, or a Snapmaker U1, or any other attractive multicolor printer without sealed filament storage. The entire experience of using a 3D printer is friendlier when you don’t have to prep the printer before printing.
Even so, it’s pretty dang tempting to save $280 or more by going with the Elegoo. But over the course of the roughly 1,000 hours I tested the Carbon and Carbon 2 side by side with the Bambu P2S, the Elegoo printers broke down in ways that were more difficult to diagnose.
The original Carbon’s extruder had some feeding issues and I found a lot of black dust inside after taking it apart, seemingly from worn plastic gears. Just this week, my Carbon 2’s stopped working after its nozzle mysteriously crashed into the bed and it refused to auto-level itself (which would normally fix that issue). I had to take the bed apart and still couldn’t find anything wrong.
In the end, yanking and reseating four tiny fragile-and-yet-too-tight connectors inside the bed fixed that problem, but it’s not the kind of solution a consumer should have to do.
Anecdotally, my Bambu printers have led a comparatively charmed life: In 1,692 hours of printing with the P2S, I’ve had to swap out the nozzle twice, clean and relubricate the traversal rods and screws several times, wash the removable magnetic printing surfaces a bunch of times with water and dish soap, and clear several filament jams in the AMS. That’s about it.
P2S nozzle replacements are easier, too. When you jam today’s Elegoo printers, you’re going old-school, either by wrenching off a hot nozzle so you can clean or inexpensively replace it ($25 for eight nozzles) or by fishing out tiny wires and unscrewing two bolts to remove an entire $30 hotend (which includes the elements that heat the plastic) at once. With Bambu’s P2S, you can just yank off a gasket and open one spring clip to swap a whole new toolless hotend ($18) in less than a minute. It does help to have a pair of mini pliers to grab the nozzle, though.
The Elegoo printers also have noisy fans that stay active even when you’re not printing, unlike the Bambu, though the Centauri Carbon 2 does shut them off more quickly than the original. Both Elegoo and Bambu let you remotely monitor your prints from its built-in camera and capture timelapse videos, but Elegoo’s camera and lighting are crap quality by comparison.
If I’m being completely honest, Bambu’s own Bambu P1S Combo, at $509 on sale, is the closest competition for the $649 P2S Combo, and I had a hunch it might be my pick in the end. I upgraded my P1P with most of the P1S upgrades, and it’s been a reliable workhorse: nearly 3,000 hours of 3D printing so far.
But over the past year, I’ve gravitated towards the P2S more and more because of its easy-swap hotends, the built-in touchscreen where I easily manage prints and rolls of filament, and all kinds of little improvements that I find I actually care about:
- It has a built-in guide that helps me put the P2S’s magnetic build plate in the right place every time, saving me from failures I’ve had with the P1P.
- It’ll automatically detect if I forget to put the build plate back, too, which saved me once this past year.
- The nozzle wiper is better at removing ooze that might wind up in your print and the poop chute clogs less.
- You don’t need to leave the door or lid open when printing PLA because it has active ventilation.
- It’s easier to add a second AMS later for four more colors, or just a single fifth roll on an external spindle.
- The stainless steel linear rods are easier to clean.
- I can sweep debris right out of the enclosure because the floor is a smooth ramp.
- The camera’s better, and video from it is far better lit.
- The AMS 2 makes it far easier to clear bits of old brittle filament without taking the unit apart.
Plus, I did have to replace the entire heatbed on my P1P once. I can’t say that nothing will go wrong with the P2S, and you shouldn’t take away that they’re as simple as an inkjet. They will need occasional maintenance, you’ll need to load good-quality filament and probably want to avoid rolls that come on lightweight cardboard (I try to buy Bambu, Sunlu, or Elegoo refills for my reusable plastic Bambu spools), and even then there will be components that wear out.
After 1,600 hours, the AMS 2 that came with my Bambu P2S review unit sometimes complains when trying to unwind or rewind some rolls of filament from some slots, and I suspect it’s because some of the gears are wearing prematurely. Bambu recently announced it’ll replace some of those gears free of charge, but only ones manufactured between May and July 2026, and even then you’ll have to be pretty handy to install them yourself.
I strongly believe people buying their first printer should get something tried and true, fully baked, simple to use, and the P2S is the best yet. But even Bambu is still catering more to DIY enthusiasts who’ll tolerate the occasional hardware defect.
So yes, if you’re asking “Which printer should I get,” I think you’d be pleasantly surprised with a P2S! But I wouldn’t blame you for waiting a few more years.

====================================================================================================

Republicans learn X is the echo chamber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:27:34 UTC
03:27:34 KST

There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”
BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.
The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.
The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.
This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.
It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.
“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a PhD candidate at Virginia Tech who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.
In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.
During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.
"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.
“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.
Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.
“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.
As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”
Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”
Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.
“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”
Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.
In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”
It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.
She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”
“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”
Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:24:28 UTC
03:24:28 KST

- Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way.
- Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated.
- We’ve open sourced everything, including the protocol, server, client through Meta’s Time library on GitHub.
- We’re also encouraging everyone, particularly those who maintain an NTP client on Android or iOS, to join us in enabling NTS support.
We’ve previously written about building a more accurate time service at Meta scale – migrating from ntpd to chrony, going from 10 milliseconds to 100 microseconds, and opening time.meta.com to everyone.
That work made time precise. This work makes it verifiable.
Why NTS?
NTP has been unauthenticated since 1985, like a lot of the internet’s foundational protocols. But it is also the one every certificate, token, and signature is checked against. The client sends 48 bytes, something sends 48 bytes back, and the client believes it. There is no signature and no identity.
It is not alone in that. Plenty of the internet’s foundational protocols were designed for a network where nobody was assumed to be hostile, and the industry has been retrofitting them ever since. What makes time different is that it is not just another protocol to secure. It is the input every other security decision is measured against.
For most of NTP’s life that did not matter much, because a clock being a few seconds off was an operational annoyance. Today it is load-bearing:
- Certificate validation: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the local clock. Wrong clock, wrong answer.
- Token and credential expiry: “Valid for 15 minutes” is a claim about a clock.
- Replay windows: Rejecting a request older than N seconds requires knowing what time it is.
- Log correlation and ordering: Two hosts that disagree produce a timeline that never happened.
And the check itself is circular. You can’t do X.509 notBefore/notAfter validation without knowing the current time. Effectively you’d have to disable cert time validation, or implement one of the suggested work-arounds.
There are two common workarounds. Both are bad. You can skip validation until the clock is set, which leaves a device unprotected exactly when it is most exposed. Or you can build in-slack: A certificate issued at 12:00:00 is rejected by a client whose clock reads 11:59:30, so issuers backdate notBefore by a few minutes and validators quietly widen the window at their end. Both sides are guessing at how wrong the other one is.
That was survivable when a certificate lasted 398 days. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 changed that. The cap on newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped to 200 days in March 2026, falls to 100 days in March 2027, and reaches 47 days in March 2029 — with domain validation reuse dropping to 10 days at the same point.
At 47 days, manual certificate management stops being viable at any scale. Renewal moves to roughly monthly, and it happens unattended — usually over ACME. An automated renewal loop on a host with a skewed clock does not raise a ticket. It reissues, or it fails, on a schedule nobody is watching.
How NTS Works
NTS works in phases, and separating them is what makes it deployable.
Phase 1 – Key Establishment (NTS-KE): TLS 1.3 over TCP/4460, negotiated with ALPN ntske/1. The client and server agree on an AEAD algorithm, then derive two directional session keys (C2S and S2C) straight from the TLS session using the RFC 5705 exporter. The server issues eight cookies, tells the client which NTP server to actually use via a server negotiation record, and closes the connection. This happens once, not per packet.
We negotiate three AEADs: AES-SIV-CMAC-256 (ID 15), which RFC 8915 makes mandatory to implement and is what an unknown client is most likely to ask for; AES-SIV-CMAC-512 (17); and AES-128-GCM-SIV (30). Client preference wins.
Phase 2 – Authenticated NTP: Standard NTPv4 over UDP/123 to the advertised server, with NTS extension fields. A request carries a unique identifier, a cookie, and an authenticator; the authenticator covers everything before it, but encrypts nothing. The server opens the cookie to recover the session keys, verifies that authenticator, and replies with the unique identifier echoed back plus an authenticator of its own – and that one does carry a payload: the fresh cookies, encrypted inside it.
A forged packet fails verification and is dropped. We do not send an NTS NAK, so a failure is indistinguishable from packet loss and cannot be used to push a client into a fresh key exchange. A replayed response carries the wrong unique identifier and matches no outstanding request. Because the replacement cookies ride inside the response authenticator rather than in the clear, an observer sees a different opaque blob every exchange and cannot follow a client between networks. Spending each cookie once is the client’s side of that bargain – the server is stateless and does not track them.
Cookies Without State
A cookie is a server state handed to the client for safekeeping. It holds the session keys, sealed with AES-SIV so only the server can open it. The obvious implementation is a key ring replicated to every server, which turns time service into a distributed state problem.
We do not replicate keys. Each server derives the sealing key from a shared master secret and the current day:
Since the Unix epoch, day is measured as whole 24-hour periods,  not a calendar day. So there is no timezone and no DST, and every host computes the same integer for the same instant. That integer is the cookie’s key ID and travels in the clear. A server that has been handed a cookie it has never seen or sealed by a host it has never talked to, re-derives the key and opens it. We accept two days back and one forward to cover skew around a rotation boundary.
The result is no key ring, no replication, no session table, no shared state to fall out of sync, and nothing for an attacker to exhaust. It is also what makes the split above work – the KE server and the NTP servers it hands you off to are different machines in different places, and they never exchange anything. Adding a server is adding a server.
The plain NTP path is untouched. The responder parses extension fields only when they are present, so unauthenticated clients hit the same code as before at the same cost.
Using NTS
One line of chrony config:
nts.meta.com terminates key exchange only. During the handshake it advertises an NTP responder in a server negotiation record, so the client is steered to time.meta.com and sends its authenticated NTP there. The host you configure is not the host you end up talking to.
That indirection is why we use pool rather than server. A single server line gives you one association and one responder, which is a single point of failure – and NTP is a protocol that wants several sources so it can outvote a bad one. pool asks for maxsources independent associations. Each runs its own key exchange over its own TLS session, so each ends up with a distinct pair of session keys:
Five rows, five independent authenticated sources, from one line of config and one KE endpoint.
Reading across: Type 30 is the negotiated AEAD, AES-128-GCM-SIV, with KLen 128 bits of session key — chrony lists it first and client preference wins. CLen 68 is the cookie: 36 bytes of envelope around the two 16-byte keys inside. Cook 8 is cookies in hand and NAK 0 means none has been rejected.
The more interesting half is not in the table. Each row’s session keys came out of its own TLS handshake and work only for that association. The key that seals them into a cookie is the shared one – the epoch day number from the derivation above, identical on every responder we run, stamped inside each cookie and never visible to the client. That split is what lets a single key exchange hand a client five different responders that have never spoken to each other.
When a pool member completes key exchange and moves to its negotiated responder, the freed KE address is handed to the next unresolved member, repeating until maxsources responders have answered. Five sources come up in about 20 minutes as each member completes its own key exchange in turn.
NTS Protects Against Attacks
Unlike NTP, NTS stops a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack from forging the answer. A classic MITM attack doesn’t need to break any cryptography, it just has to answer a client before a real server does. If an attacker rolls the clock backward they can make expired certificates validate again or revoked tokens work again. Any control that relies on something having expired is reset. If they roll the clock forward everything expires at once. This is the more difficult direction to address because beyond a certain point the failure stops being recoverable.
Let’s look at an example of what happens to a device that gets convinced it is the year 2037. NTP counts seconds in a 32-bit field that wraps in February 2036, and a client stranded on the far side of that boundary computes its correction into the wrong era – so the mechanism that exists to fix a wrong clock now moves it further away. Meanwhile every certificate the device holds is long expired, so TLS fails, therefore it cannot reach anything that might help, including its own update service. The patch that would fix it cannot be delivered, because delivering it needs the clock that is broken.
The device is not damaged. Every component works exactly as designed. It is simply holding a number that puts it outside the reach of the network. And no amount of waiting or rebooting fixes it. Recovery means a factory reset, or a trip to a service center. Multiply that by a fleet and the cost of a wrong integer becomes a logistics problem.
Now, consider a clock forward attack on a host that issues credentials. Short-lived credentials are considered safe because they expire quickly, which means short lifetime is doing the job revocation would otherwise do. That property is entirely a function of the issuing host’s clock. An issuer convinced it is next year signs credentials that outlive the window you designed for.
What NTS Does Not Fix
Delay attacks. RFC 8915 is explicit. An attacker who holds your packets shifts your clock by up to half the delay introduced, and no cryptography in the protocol detects it, because every byte is genuine. Authentication tells you who wrote a packet, not how long it spent in flight. Mitigations are the usual ones – multiple independent sources, sanity limits, bounded steps.
So the claim is narrow: An on-path attacker can still delay your packets and can still drop them. What they can no longer do is lie about the contents.
Bootstrapping. NTS-KE runs over TLS and TLS wants a working clock, which is the same circular problem as above. A device with a dead RTC still has to get roughly correct before its first handshake.
Wrong servers. NTS authenticates the path, not the answer. A server that is correctly configured, correctly authenticated, and simply wrong will hand you the wrong time with a perfect signature on it. Quorum, sanity checks, and monitoring are still required.
Monotonicity. Authenticated time is still wall-clock time, and wall clocks move backward — at a leap second, or whenever a correction lands. Cloudflare’s authoritative DNS hit this at the end of 2016: a resolver round-trip measured across the leap second came out negative, propagated into upstream selection, and panicked Go’s rand.Int63n(). Nothing was forged and nothing was misdelivered. If your code measures elapsed time, use a monotonic clock.
Adoption
RFC 8915, Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol, was published on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard in September 2020. Cloudflare had launched time.cloudflare.com with NTS 15 months earlier, in June 2019, against the then-current draft, and showed it works at scale.
Server-side, the public NTS list today runs to a few dozen entries, mostly national metrology institutes and internet infrastructure operators such as PTB, Netnod, and time.nl. We are adding one more.
The bigger gap is on the client. NTS support exists where you would expect it in the server world – chrony and ntpsec implement it. It is absent entirely from the stock time client on the platforms that account for most of the endpoints on the internet.
Android’s platform time sync is plain SNTP over UDP/123 – a fixed 48-byte packet with no extension-field handling, alongside NITZ and GNSS – so there is no NTS path in it. Apple devices sync through timed against time.apple.com, where we are not aware of any NTS support either.
Those two stacks set the clock on billions of phones, watches and headsets, and every one of them is trusting an unauthenticated UDP packet. A device vendor can ship a separate NTS-capable client today — chrony runs perfectly well on Android – but that is a workaround for something the platform should do itself.
The protocol is finished, the servers are appearing, the client implementations exist.
What is missing is mobile.
Join Us in Enabling NTS
nts.meta.com is live and free. The code is in github.com/facebook/time.
If you run a public time service, turn NTS on. If you maintain an NTP client, implement RFC 8915. If you own the time stack in a mobile OS, this is the gap – Android and iOS are where most of the world’s clocks get set, and both of them are still doing it over an unauthenticated packet.
We have spent years making time more precise. Precision without authenticity only gets you a very accurate number from an unknown source. Now it can be both.

We’d like to thank Sofia Scalzo, Pablo Mazzini, Vadim Fedorenko, Patrick Cullen, and Yixin Wei for their support on this project.

OpenAI president Greg Brockman says company could be IPO ready in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-05
18:02:27 UTC
03:02:27 KST

OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said the company would be ready for an IPO in 2027, noting that its enterprise revenue has been growing. Speaking at a Wall Street Journal tech conference on Wednesday, the executive touted how the company had been gaining ground in the enterprise market, where rival Anthropic had already successfully made inroads.
In response to the interviewer’s question about being IPO-ready next year, Brockman replied, “I think so. Yes.”
“We’ve been very clear this year that we want to go public when we feel is the right time for us, and I feel extremely good about the business. I feel like we’ve made so much progress this year, and I’ve honestly never felt more confident in what we’re doing,” Brockman said.
He detailed how OpenAI’s trajectory as an enterprise had changed over the course of 2026, noting that the first and second quarters were “pretty rough.” He also admitted that OpenAI “wasn’t even in the conversation” when it came to agentic coding — an area where Anthropic’s Claude Code has gained market share.
“We had Codex, but no one was talking about it,” Brockman continued, “and I think that we just kept our heads down and executed.”
By the third quarter, activity picked up, as OpenAI saw 70% quarterly growth in its annualized revenue — something Brockman attributed to the enterprise side of the business doubling. He explained that the growth wasn’t simply the result of something that happened in the quarter itself, but rather the culmination of investments the company had been making up to that point.
Now the majority of OpenAI’s revenue is coming from the enterprise business, which previously accounted for only around 30% of its total revenue.
“And it’s not that consumer [revenue has shrunk] … It’s been growing, but it’s the enterprise segment has really taken off,” he said, pointing to a recent partnership with JPMorgan Chase as one example of the type of client it’s now winning deals with.
Brockman also spoke more broadly about the lessons OpenAI learned from selling into the enterprise market as well. He said the company had come to understand that its job was to help businesses identify the most important milestones they could achieve with its AI technology, build trust with clients, and demonstrate that it was a reliable partner for the long haul.
“A year ago, we weren’t even really in the enterprise game, right? We were really perceived as a consumer company, and a lot of the companies we’d start talking to would say, ‘Is OpenAI really committed to the enterprise?’” Brockman said. “But it’s so different today.”
